subtopics.title: Semiconductor Devices
subtopics.subtitle: From the pn junction to CMOS logic: a roadmap of the devices this topic covers

concepts.text: What This Topic Covers

Semiconductor devices are components whose conduction is set by doping and by the voltages applied to their junctions, not by a fixed resistance. Section 1.4 of the NEC syllabus builds up from the physics of silicon and germanium to the pn-junction diode, the bipolar junction transistor (BJT), the MOSFET and finally CMOS logic. Together these devices form the basis of rectifiers, regulators, amplifiers, switches and every digital integrated circuit.
Roadmap of the five subtopics:
items: Semiconductor Basics: intrinsic and extrinsic material, energy bands, doping, majority and minority carriers, silicon versus germanium.
Semiconductor Diode: pn-junction formation, forward and reverse bias, V-I characteristic, Shockley equation, special diodes and applications.
BJT: npn and pnp structure, alpha and beta, CB/CE/CC configurations, cut-off, active and saturation regions.
MOSFET: insulated gate, enhancement and depletion types, threshold voltage, square-law saturation current, comparison with JFET and BJT.
CMOS: complementary nMOS-pMOS pair, the inverter, near-zero static power, noise margins, CMOS versus TTL.

concepts.text: The Device Family Tree

Every device here is built from the same two ingredients, p-type and n-type silicon. One junction gives a diode, which conducts in one direction only. Two back-to-back junctions give a BJT, in which a small base current controls a much larger collector current. Replacing the base contact with an insulated gate gives the MOSFET, in which a gate voltage controls the channel current while drawing almost no gate current. Pairing an n-channel with a p-channel MOSFET gives CMOS, the structure used in almost every microprocessor and memory chip.
Key Terms to Know First
Terms you will meet in every subtopic of this section:
items: Majority and minority carriers: the dominant and the scarce charge carriers in a doped semiconductor (electrons and holes respectively in n-type, the reverse in p-type).
Depletion region and barrier potential: the carrier-free zone at a pn junction and its built-in voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium.
Forward and reverse bias: the polarity that narrows the depletion region and allows current, or widens it and blocks current.
Alpha and beta: the BJT current gains I_C/I_E (slightly below 1) and I_C/I_B (typically 50 to 300).
Threshold voltage V_T: the minimum gate-source voltage that creates a channel in an enhancement MOSFET.
Current-controlled versus voltage-controlled: BJT versus FET, the most frequently tested contrast in this topic.

concepts.text: How the Exam Tests This Area
Typical MCQ patterns:
items: Device identification: which diode regulates voltage, which one emits light, which device has an insulated gate, which one is unipolar.
Biasing conditions: which junctions are forward or reverse biased in each BJT region, and which MOSFET type conducts at V_GS = 0.
Alpha-beta arithmetic: convert between the two gains, or find I_B and I_C from a given I_E.
Contrasts: BJT versus MOSFET, MOSFET versus JFET, CMOS versus TTL, enhancement versus depletion mode.
Standard values: 0.7 V and 0.3 V drops, 26 mV thermal voltage, band gaps of 1.1 eV (Si) and 0.72 eV (Ge).

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Device Families, Ratings and Data Sheets
Semiconductor devices can be classified in several independent ways, and a question may use any of them:
items: By number of junctions or layers: one pn junction (diode), two junctions (BJT), three junctions in a pnpn stack (SCR or thyristor), no junction in the current path (the MOSFET channel, the Schottky metal-semiconductor contact).

By carriers: bipolar or minority-carrier devices (pn diode, BJT, SCR) rely on both electrons and holes; unipolar or majority-carrier devices (JFET, MOSFET, Schottky diode) use only one type, so they store almost no charge and switch faster.
By control: two-terminal devices have no control input; the BJT is current-controlled; JFETs, MOSFETs and IGBTs are voltage-controlled.
By power level: small-signal devices (milliwatts, used in amplifiers and logic) versus power devices (watts to kilowatts, used in converters and motor drives), which need heat sinks.

concepts.text: A data sheet has two distinct parts. The absolute maximum ratings are limits that must never be exceeded, even briefly; operating a device at them gives no safety margin. The electrical characteristics are measured values (minimum, typical, maximum) at stated test conditions, such as h_FE at a given I_C and V_CE. Power ratings are normally quoted at 25 °C, and above that temperature the permissible dissipation is derated linearly: P_D(T) = P_D(25 °C) − k(T − 25), where the derating factor k (in W/°C, often quoted in mW/°C) equals 1/θ_JA, so that P_D(25 °C) = (T_J(max) − 25)/θ_JA.

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: choosing a heat sink
Given: P_D = 15 W, T_J(max) = 150 °C, T_A = 45 °C
       theta_JC = 1.2 °C/W, theta_CS = 0.3 °C/W
Step 1: total theta allowed = (150 - 45) / 15 = 7.0 °C/W
Step 2: theta_SA <= 7.0 - 1.2 - 0.3 = 5.5 °C/W
Step 3: pick a 4.5 °C/W heat sink (below the limit)
Check : T_J = 45 + 15 x (1.2 + 0.3 + 4.5) = 45 + 90 = 135 °C
Result: 135 °C < 150 °C, so the design is safe

concepts.latex: P_{BJT} = V_{CE(sat)} I_C + V_{BE(sat)} I_B, \quad P_{MOS} = I_D^2 R_{DS(on)}
concepts.plainText: P_BJT = VCE(sat) x IC + VBE(sat) x IB;   P_MOS = ID^2 x RDS(on)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: BJT or MOSFET as a 10 A switch?
BJT   : V_CE(sat) = 0.4 V, forced beta = 10 -> I_B = 1 A, V_BE(sat) = 1.0 V
        P = 0.4 x 10 + 1.0 x 1 = 4 + 1 = 5 W
MOSFET: R_DS(on) = 0.015 ohm, gate current negligible
        P = 10^2 x 0.015 = 1.5 W
Break-even (collector loss only): I^2 x 0.015 = 0.4 x I
        I = 0.4 / 0.015 = 26.7 A
Below about 27 A the MOSFET has the lower conduction loss;
the MOSFET loss grows as I^2, the BJT loss roughly as I.
Common mistakes with ratings and device comparisons:
items: Using the 25 °C power rating at a higher ambient temperature without derating it first.
Adding only the heat-sink thermal resistance and forgetting θ_JC and θ_CS, which are always in series with it.
Assuming V_CEO equals V_CBO; with the base open the collector leakage is multiplied by β, so V_CEO is lower.
Designing for the typical h_FE; a robust bias circuit must work over the full minimum-to-maximum spread.
Treating a MOSFET as lossless when on; R_DS(on) roughly doubles between 25 °C and 150 °C.

concepts.text: A MOSFET gate oxide is only tens of nanometres thick and is destroyed if V_GS exceeds its rating (typically about ±20 V). Static charge from handling easily reaches thousands of volts, so MOSFETs and CMOS ICs are stored in conductive packaging and handled with earthing straps.

For thermal problems write one line: T_J = T_A + P × (sum of all thermal resistances in the path). For derating, subtract k × (T − 25) from the 25 °C rating. For switch losses, BJT loss is V_CE(sat) × I_C (plus base drive) and MOSFET loss is I² × R_DS(on).

formulas.plainText: beta = IC / IB;   alpha = IC / IE
alpha = beta / (1 + beta);   beta = alpha / (1 - alpha)

notes.text: Learn the devices as a ladder: diode (one junction), BJT (two junctions, current-controlled), MOSFET (insulated gate, voltage-controlled), CMOS (a complementary MOSFET pair). Most overview questions only ask you to place a device correctly on this ladder.

Two different quantities share the symbol V_T. In the diode equation V_T is the thermal voltage, about 26 mV; for a MOSFET V_T is the threshold voltage, typically 0.5 V to 2 V. Read the context of the question before substituting numbers.
Standard values used throughout this topic: silicon forward drop 0.7 V, germanium 0.3 V, thermal voltage 26 mV at 300 K, silicon band gap 1.1 eV, germanium band gap 0.72 eV.

formulas.title: BJT Current Gains
formulas.plainText: beta = IC / IB;   alpha = IC / IE
formulas.description: Common-emitter gain beta (typically 50 to 300) and common-base gain alpha (slightly less than 1) of a BJT in the active region.

formulas.title: Alpha-Beta Conversion
formulas.plainText: alpha = beta / (1 + beta);   beta = alpha / (1 - alpha)
formulas.description: Converts between the two BJT current gains; both relations follow from IE = IB + IC.

flashcards.front: Which transistor family is current-controlled and which is voltage-controlled?
flashcards.back: The BJT is current-controlled: base current sets collector current. FETs, including the MOSFET, are voltage-controlled: gate-source voltage sets drain current with almost no gate current.

flashcards.front: Name the three terminals of a BJT and of a MOSFET.
flashcards.back: BJT: emitter, base, collector. MOSFET: source, gate, drain, plus the body (substrate), which is usually tied to the source.

flashcards.front: What does 'complementary' mean in CMOS?
flashcards.back: Each gate uses both an n-channel and a p-channel MOSFET, so in steady state one is on and the other is off and almost no supply current flows.

questions.questionText: Which device has a gate that is insulated from the channel by a thin oxide layer and therefore draws practically no steady gate current?
questions.explanation: In a MOSFET the gate is separated from the channel by a SiO2 layer, so only picoampere leakage flows. A JFET gate is a reverse-biased pn junction, not an insulator, and a BJT base carries a real bias current.

questions.questionText: In a BJT the collector current is 4.95 mA when the emitter current is 5 mA. The common-emitter current gain β is:
questions.explanation: I_B = I_E − I_C = 0.05 mA, so β = I_C/I_B = 4.95/0.05 = 99. Equivalently α = 4.95/5 = 0.99 and β = α/(1 − α) = 99.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of a device with its controlling quantity is correct?
questions.explanation: All FETs, including the JFET, are voltage-controlled: the gate-source voltage sets the drain current. The BJT is controlled by base current and a diode has no control terminal at all.

questions.questionText: The three main terminals of a MOSFET are called:
questions.explanation: A MOSFET has a gate, a source and a drain (plus a body connection). Emitter, base and collector belong to the BJT; anode and cathode to a diode or thyristor.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a unipolar device, in which current is carried by only one type of charge carrier?
questions.explanation: In a FET the channel current is carried only by majority carriers (electrons in an n-channel device, holes in a p-channel device). BJTs, pn diodes and SCRs all depend on both electrons and holes crossing junctions.

questions.questionText: A small-signal transistor is rated P_D = 625 mW at 25 °C ambient and is derated linearly at 5 mW/°C above 25 °C. Its maximum permissible dissipation at 75 °C ambient is:
questions.explanation: P_D(75 °C) = 625 − 5 × (75 − 25) = 625 − 250 = 375 mW. Subtracting 5 × 75 instead of 5 × 50 gives the wrong 250 mW.

questions.questionText: A four-layer pnpn device with three junctions, used for controlled rectification, is the:
questions.explanation: The SCR is a pnpn structure with three junctions; a gate pulse latches it on. A BJT has three layers and two junctions, and a Zener diode has one junction.

questions.questionText: A device with a junction-to-ambient thermal resistance θ_JA = 200 °C/W dissipates 0.4 W in an ambient of 30 °C. Its junction temperature is:
questions.explanation: T_J = T_A + P θ_JA = 30 + 0.4 × 200 = 30 + 80 = 110 °C. The 80 °C figure is only the temperature rise, before adding the ambient.

questions.questionText: Among the following, which device offers the highest DC input resistance at its control terminal?
questions.explanation: The oxide-insulated MOSFET gate has an input resistance of 10^12 Ω or more. A JFET gate is a reverse-biased junction, about 10^9 Ω; a BJT input is only kilohms (CE) or tens of ohms (CB).

questions.questionText: Thermal runaway is a failure mechanism mainly associated with:
options: MOSFETs, because their R_DS(on) falls sharply as they heat up
Metal-film resistors, because their resistance rises with temperature
Bipolar junction transistors, because rising temperature increases collector current, which raises the temperature further
questions.explanation: In a BJT, heating lowers V_BE and raises leakage and β, so collector current and dissipation increase, which heats the junction further. A MOSFET's R_DS(on) rises with temperature, which opposes runaway.

questions.questionText: A power transistor has T_J(max) = 150 °C, θ_JC = 1.5 °C/W, case-to-sink θ_CS = 0.5 °C/W and heat-sink θ_SA = 3 °C/W. At an ambient of 40 °C, the maximum power it can dissipate continuously is:
questions.explanation: Total θ = 1.5 + 0.5 + 3 = 5 °C/W, so P = (150 − 40)/5 = 110/5 = 22 W. Using θ_JC alone gives 73.3 W and ignoring the ambient gives 30 W.

questions.questionText: Power MOSFETs can be connected in parallel to share a large current more easily than BJTs because:
options: Their threshold voltages are exactly identical from device to device
R_DS(on) increases with temperature, so a hotter device automatically takes less current
Their gates draw large currents that balance the devices
They have a negative temperature coefficient of on-state resistance
questions.explanation: A MOSFET that carries more current heats up, its R_DS(on) rises and current shifts to the cooler devices, so sharing is self-correcting. BJTs have the opposite tendency, so they need emitter ballast resistors.

questions.questionText: A device dissipates 10 W with T_J(max) = 125 °C at an ambient of 25 °C. Given θ_JC = 2 °C/W and θ_CS = 1 °C/W, the largest heat-sink thermal resistance θ_SA that may be used is:
questions.explanation: Total allowed θ = (125 − 25)/10 = 10 °C/W; θ_SA = 10 − 2 − 1 = 7 °C/W. Forgetting θ_CS gives 8 °C/W and forgetting θ_JC gives 9 °C/W.

questions.questionText: A Schottky diode switches faster than an ordinary pn-junction diode mainly because:
options: It is a majority-carrier device, so almost no minority charge is stored that must be removed at turn-off
It has a larger band gap than silicon
Its forward drop is higher, about 1.5 V
It is always made from germanium
questions.explanation: A metal-semiconductor junction conducts by majority carriers, so there is practically no stored minority charge and hence negligible reverse-recovery time. Its forward drop is lower (about 0.2 to 0.4 V), not higher.

questions.questionText: A MOSFET switch with R_DS(on) = 0.05 Ω carries a steady drain current of 10 A. Its conduction loss is:
questions.explanation: P = I² R_DS(on) = 10² × 0.05 = 5 W. Multiplying I × R gives the voltage drop, 0.5 V, not the power.

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing a BJT with a MOSFET is NOT correct?
options: A MOSFET is a majority-carrier device, whereas a BJT uses both carrier types
At the same bias current, a BJT usually has a higher transconductance than a MOSFET
A BJT has a higher input impedance than a MOSFET
A MOSFET gate draws practically no DC current
questions.explanation: The MOSFET, with its insulated gate, has by far the higher input impedance; the BJT base draws real current. The other three statements are correct.

questions.questionText: A load current of 5 A is switched either by a BJT (V_CE(sat) = 0.3 V, needing I_B = 0.25 A at V_BE(sat) = 0.9 V) or by a MOSFET (R_DS(on) = 0.02 Ω, negligible gate current). By how much does the BJT's total on-state loss (collector plus base) exceed the MOSFET's?
questions.explanation: BJT: 0.3 × 5 + 0.9 × 0.25 = 1.5 + 0.225 = 1.725 W. MOSFET: 5² × 0.02 = 0.5 W. Difference = 1.725 − 0.5 = 1.225 W (ignoring the base drive gives 1.0 W).

questions.questionText: On a rectifier diode data sheet, the rating V_RRM denotes the:
options: Maximum repetitive peak reverse voltage the diode can withstand
Forward voltage drop at rated current
questions.explanation: V_RRM is the repetitive peak reverse voltage, the data-sheet form of the peak inverse voltage (PIV) rating. Forward drop is V_F, recovery time is t_rr and surge current is I_FSM.

questions.questionText: A rectifier diode in a half-wave circuit is fed directly from a 230 V (rms) sinusoidal supply. Allowing a safety factor of 1.5 on the peak inverse voltage, the minimum V_RRM rating to select is about:
questions.explanation: Peak inverse voltage = V_m = 230√2 = 325 V; with the safety factor 1.5 × 325 = 488 V. Forgetting √2 gives 345 V; using 2V_m (centre-tapped full-wave) gives 976 V.

questions.questionText: For a given BJT, how does the collector-emitter breakdown rating V_CEO (base open) compare with the collector-base rating V_CBO (emitter open)?
options: V_CEO is zero because the base is open
questions.explanation: With the base open, the collector-base leakage acts as base current and is multiplied by β, so avalanche breakdown sets in at a lower voltage. Data sheets therefore always show V_CEO below V_CBO.

questions.questionText: A BJT data sheet quotes a transition frequency f_T = 300 MHz and a low-frequency β of 150. The β cut-off frequency f_β, at which β has fallen by 3 dB, is about:
questions.explanation: f_T ≈ β₀ f_β, so f_β = f_T/β₀ = 300 MHz/150 = 2 MHz. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 45 GHz.

questions.questionText: The 'absolute maximum ratings' listed on a transistor data sheet are best described as:
options: Typical values at which the device should normally be operated
Limits that must never be exceeded, even momentarily; they are not recommended operating conditions
Values measured at the point of highest efficiency
questions.explanation: Absolute maximum ratings are stress limits beyond which damage may occur; a good design keeps well inside them. Typical and guaranteed performance figures appear separately under electrical characteristics.

questions.questionText: A BJT has f_T = 300 MHz and a low-frequency β of 150. At a signal frequency of 10 MHz, well above its β cut-off, the magnitude of its common-emitter current gain is approximately:
questions.explanation: Above f_β the gain falls in inverse proportion to frequency, |β| ≈ f_T/f = 300/10 = 30. (The exact value 150/√(1 + 5²) = 29.4 confirms this.)

questions.questionText: Which pairing of a device with its principal application is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: A photodiode detects light: it is reverse-biased and its current rises with illumination. Light emission is the job of an LED. The other three pairings are correct.

questions.questionText: At a bias current of 1 mA, a BJT (V_T = 26 mV) is compared with a MOSFET in saturation that follows the square law and operates at an overdrive voltage V_GS − V_th = 0.2 V. The ratio g_m(BJT)/g_m(MOSFET) is about:
questions.explanation: BJT: g_m = I_C/V_T = 1 mA/26 mV = 38.5 mA/V. MOSFET: g_m = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_th) = 2 × 1/0.2 = 10 mA/V. Ratio = 38.5/10 = 3.85 (dropping the factor 2 gives 7.7).

questions.questionText: The transition frequency f_T quoted on a BJT data sheet is the frequency at which:
options: The common-base gain α falls to 0.707 of its low-frequency value
The common-emitter short-circuit current gain falls to 1
The voltage gain of any amplifier falls by 3 dB
questions.explanation: f_T is the unity-gain frequency of the short-circuit CE current gain, and f_T ≈ β₀ f_β. The frequency at which α falls by 3 dB is a different figure, f_α.

questions.questionText: A red LED has V_F = 2 V at its rated forward current I_F = 15 mA. The series resistor needed to run it at rated current from a 5 V supply is:
questions.explanation: R = (V_S − V_F)/I_F = (5 − 2)/0.015 = 200 Ω. Ignoring V_F gives 333 Ω; using V_F alone gives 133 Ω.

questions.questionText: On a power MOSFET data sheet, R_DS(on) is:
options: The DC resistance of the gate input
The resistance of the body diode when reverse-biased
The drain-source resistance when the device is fully turned on at a specified V_GS
questions.explanation: R_DS(on) is the on-state drain-source resistance at a stated V_GS (for example 10 V) and drain current; it sets the conduction loss I²R_DS(on). With V_GS = 0 an enhancement MOSFET is off.

questions.questionText: A 5.1 V Zener diode has a power rating of 500 mW. The maximum Zener current it can safely carry is about:
questions.explanation: I_Z(max) = P_Z/V_Z = 0.5/5.1 = 0.098 A = 98 mA. Multiplying P by V gives the meaningless 2.55.

questions.questionText: The parameter V_GS(th) on an enhancement MOSFET data sheet specifies:
options: The maximum gate-source voltage before oxide breakdown
The gate-source voltage that gives the lowest R_DS(on)
The gate-source voltage at which the drain current reaches a small specified value, marking the start of conduction
questions.explanation: V_GS(th) is measured as the V_GS that gives a small drain current such as 250 µA. The oxide limit is V_GS(max), and full enhancement needs V_GS well above V_GS(th).

questions.questionText: A silicon diode's reverse leakage current is 10 nA at 25 °C. Using the rule that leakage current doubles for every 10 °C rise, the leakage at 75 °C is:
questions.explanation: A 50 °C rise is five doublings: I_R = 10 × 2^5 = 320 nA. Multiplying by 5 instead of 2^5 gives 50 nA.

questions.questionText: Which device is the basic building block of almost all present-day microprocessors and memory chips?
options: The MOSFET, used in CMOS circuits
questions.explanation: CMOS logic, built from complementary n- and p-channel MOSFETs, dominates digital ICs because of its very low static power and high packing density.

questions.questionText: A silicon BJT has V_BE = 0.70 V at 25 °C for a fixed collector current. Taking a temperature coefficient of −2 mV/°C, its V_BE at 100 °C is:
questions.explanation: ΔV_BE = −2 mV/°C × (100 − 25) °C = −150 mV, so V_BE = 0.70 − 0.15 = 0.55 V. Adding instead of subtracting gives 0.85 V; using a 100 °C rise gives 0.50 V.

questions.questionText: MOSFETs must be handled with anti-static precautions mainly because:
options: The very thin gate oxide can be punctured by static voltages far above its V_GS rating (typically about ±20 V)
Static charge forward-biases the drain-source junction permanently
Static charge permanently changes the doping of the channel
The body diode stores static charge and later discharges into the load
questions.explanation: The gate oxide is only tens of nanometres thick, so a few tens of volts can rupture it, while static discharges from handling reach thousands of volts. The damage is permanent.

questions.questionText: A MOSFET has R_DS(on) = 0.04 Ω at 25 °C, and its data sheet shows R_DS(on) rising by a factor of 1.6 at a junction temperature of 125 °C. At 8 A drain current, the conduction loss at 125 °C is about:
questions.explanation: R_DS(on) at 125 °C = 1.6 × 0.04 = 0.064 Ω; P = 8² × 0.064 = 4.1 W. The 25 °C value gives 2.56 W and dividing by 1.6 gives 1.6 W.

questions.questionText: An IGBT (insulated-gate bipolar transistor) combines:
options: The current drive of a BJT with the zero stored charge of a Schottky diode
Two pn diodes connected back to back
A JFET input with a four-layer thyristor latch that cannot be turned off
The insulated-gate voltage drive of a MOSFET with the low on-state voltage of a bipolar output at high current
questions.explanation: An IGBT has a MOSFET-style insulated gate (easy voltage drive, negligible gate current) controlling a bipolar conduction path, giving a low forward drop at high current. It is widely used in inverters and motor drives.

questions.questionText: A transistor has P_D(max) = 250 mW at its operating temperature. Which operating point (V_CE, I_C) keeps the collector dissipation within this rating?
questions.explanation: Collector dissipation ≈ V_CE I_C: 5 × 40 = 200 mW (within rating), while 10 × 30 = 300 mW, 12 × 25 = 300 mW and 8 × 35 = 280 mW all exceed 250 mW.

questions.questionText: For a 48 V DC-DC converter switching at 500 kHz, the most suitable switching device is usually a:
questions.explanation: A power MOSFET is a majority-carrier device with no storage time and needs only a voltage gate drive, so it can switch at hundreds of kilohertz. An SCR cannot be turned off from its gate and is far too slow.

questions.questionText: The storage time that slows the turn-off of a saturated BJT switch is caused by:
options: Majority carriers trapped in the emitter contact
Excess minority carriers stored in the base that must be removed before the collector current can fall
The thermal time constant of the heat sink
questions.explanation: In saturation both junctions are forward-biased and excess minority charge builds up in the base; until it is swept out or recombines the transistor stays on. MOSFETs have no such stored charge.

questions.questionText: A transistor is rated 1.2 W at 25 °C and derated at 8 mW/°C above 25 °C. If it operates at V_CE = 10 V in a 60 °C ambient, the maximum allowable collector current is:
questions.explanation: P_D(60 °C) = 1.2 − 0.008 × (60 − 25) = 1.2 − 0.28 = 0.92 W; I_C = 0.92/10 = 92 mA. Without derating, 120 mA; derating over the full 60 °C gives 72 mA.

questions.questionText: Which data-sheet parameter best indicates how quickly a rectifier diode can change from conducting to blocking?
questions.explanation: t_rr is the time taken to remove the stored charge after the diode is reverse-biased. Fast-recovery and Schottky diodes are chosen for high-frequency rectification because of their small t_rr.

questions.questionText: A rectifier diode with a forward drop of about 1 V carries an average forward current of 2 A. Its approximate power dissipation is:
questions.explanation: Diode loss ≈ V_F × I_F(AV) = 1 × 2 = 2 W. This is why rectifiers carrying several amperes need a heat sink.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the JFET is correct?
options: Its gate is a reverse-biased pn junction and it operates only in depletion mode
Its gate is insulated from the channel by an oxide layer
It is normally off at V_GS = 0
It is a bipolar, minority-carrier device
questions.explanation: The JFET gate-channel junction is kept reverse-biased; V_GS = 0 gives the maximum current I_DSS and making V_GS more negative (n-channel) narrows the channel. An oxide-insulated gate belongs to the MOSFET.

questions.questionText: A power MOSFET has a total gate charge Q_g = 20 nC. When it is switched on and off at 100 kHz, the average current the gate driver must supply is:
questions.explanation: Each cycle the driver delivers Q_g, so I_avg = Q_g × f = 20 × 10^-9 × 10^5 = 2 × 10^-3 A = 2 mA. The DC gate current is negligible, but switching still needs this charge.

questions.questionText: The safe operating area (SOA) of a power BJT is bounded by the maximum collector current, the maximum V_CE, the maximum power dissipation and:
questions.explanation: Second breakdown is a localised current crowding and hot-spot failure at high V_CE that limits the BJT SOA below the power-dissipation line. Threshold voltage and gate oxide apply to MOSFETs.

questions.questionText: As the junction temperature of silicon devices rises, which of the following changes is NOT correct?
options: The forward voltage of a diode at fixed current decreases
The reverse leakage current of a diode increases
The R_DS(on) of a MOSFET decreases
The V_BE of a BJT at fixed collector current decreases
questions.explanation: R_DS(on) increases with temperature because carrier mobility falls. The other three statements are correct: forward drops fall by about 2 mV/°C and leakage roughly doubles every 10 °C.

questions.questionText: A MOSFET switches a 5 A load from a 48 V supply at 100 kHz. The combined rise and fall time is 100 ns. Using P_sw ≈ ½ V I (t_r + t_f) f, the switching loss is about:
Which of these devices is normally OFF, conducting only after its gate-source voltage exceeds a threshold?
questions.explanation: An enhancement MOSFET has no channel until V_GS exceeds V_GS(th). Depletion MOSFETs and JFETs of either polarity have a channel at V_GS = 0 and are normally on.

questions.questionText: A transistor data sheet gives h_FE as minimum 100 and maximum 300 at I_C = 10 mA. A good bias design should:
options: Assume β is exactly 200, the average of the limits
Assume β = 300, because that is the rated value
Work correctly for any β in that range, so the Q-point must not depend strongly on β
Ignore β, because it has no effect on the collector current in any circuit
questions.explanation: h_FE varies widely between samples and with temperature, so the data sheet gives a spread. Stable bias circuits such as voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor make the Q-point nearly independent of β.

questions.questionText: The junction-to-ambient thermal resistance θ_JA of a device, in °C/W, tells you:
options: The maximum power the device can dissipate
The temperature at which the device fails
How much the device current rises for each degree of temperature
How many degrees the junction rises above ambient for each watt dissipated
questions.explanation: θ_JA is the temperature rise per watt: T_J − T_A = P θ_JA. A lower θ_JA, achieved with a bigger package or a heat sink, lets the device dissipate more power.

subtopics.title: Semiconductor Basics
subtopics.subtitle: Energy bands, intrinsic and extrinsic material, doping, carriers and transport

concepts.text: Semiconductor Basics

Intrinsic: a pure semiconductor (e.g. pure Si or Ge) with equal numbers of free electrons and holes.
N-type: doped with a pentavalent impurity (e.g. phosphorus); the majority carriers are electrons.
P-type: doped with a trivalent impurity (e.g. boron); the majority carriers are holes.
Covalent Bonding, Energy Bands and Band Gap

Silicon and germanium are tetravalent: each atom shares its four valence electrons with four neighbours, forming a covalent crystal with no free carriers at absolute zero. At room temperature thermal energy breaks a few bonds, releasing a free electron and leaving a vacancy, or hole, that behaves as a positive carrier. Electrons and holes are generated in pairs, so in intrinsic material n = p = n_i, about 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³ for silicon at 300 K. When a free electron falls back into a hole the pair disappears; this is recombination.

In a solid the allowed electron energies form bands. The valence band holds the bonding electrons and the conduction band holds electrons that are free to move; the forbidden gap between them is the band gap E_g. In a conductor the two bands overlap, so electrons flow with no extra energy. In an insulator the gap is large (more than about 5 eV) and practically no electrons cross it. A semiconductor has a small gap, about 1.1 eV for silicon and 0.72 eV for germanium, so room-temperature thermal energy lifts a useful number of electrons into the conduction band.

rows: Very high, falls as temperature rises

concepts.text: Doping: N-type and P-type
Adding a controlled impurity, roughly one atom in a million, changes the conductivity by many orders of magnitude and makes the material extrinsic:
items: N-type: a pentavalent donor (phosphorus, arsenic or antimony) bonds with four neighbours and donates its fifth electron to the conduction band. Electrons are the majority carriers and holes the minority; each ionised donor is a fixed positive charge.

P-type: a trivalent acceptor (boron, aluminium, gallium or indium) has only three valence electrons, so one bond is incomplete. It accepts an electron from a neighbour, creating a hole. Holes are the majority carriers and electrons the minority; each ionised acceptor is a fixed negative charge.
Both types stay electrically neutral overall, because the fixed impurity ions exactly balance the free majority carriers.

concepts.text: Carrier Concentrations, Drift and Diffusion

In thermal equilibrium the product of the electron and hole concentrations is fixed for a given material and temperature, whatever the doping: this is the mass-action law. Adding donors raises n and lowers p by the same factor, so heavily doped material has very few minority carriers. For a typical silicon doping of 10^16 donors per cm³ the electron concentration is about 10^16 per cm³, while the hole concentration falls to about 2.25 × 10^4 per cm³.

concepts.plainText: n x p = ni^2   (mass-action law)

concepts.text: Two mechanisms move carriers. Drift is motion under an electric field: the drift velocity v_d = μE is proportional to the field through the mobility μ, and the conductivity is σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p). Diffusion is motion from a region of high carrier concentration to one of low concentration, with no field needed; it is the process that forms the depletion region of a pn junction. Electrons are more mobile than holes (in silicon roughly 1350 against 480 cm²/V·s), which is one reason n-channel devices are faster than p-channel ones.
Silicon versus Germanium and the Effect of Temperature

Silicon dominates because its larger band gap gives a leakage current about a thousand times smaller than germanium, it tolerates junction temperatures of 150 to 200 °C against 75 to 100 °C for germanium, it is abundant, and it grows a stable native oxide (SiO₂) that is essential for MOSFETs. Germanium offers higher carrier mobility and a lower forward drop of 0.3 V, so it survives in a few high-frequency and low-drop applications. In both materials raising the temperature generates more electron-hole pairs, so resistance falls: semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance, the opposite of metals.
Going Deeper: Carrier Statistics and Transport

The shortcut n ≈ N_D rests on two facts. At room temperature practically every donor and acceptor is ionised, and the crystal must stay electrically neutral, so the positive charges (holes plus ionised donors) equal the negative charges (electrons plus ionised acceptors): p + N_D = n + N_A. Combining this with the mass-action law gives a quadratic in n whose exact solution is shown below. When the net doping |N_D − N_A| is much larger than n_i, the square root collapses and n ≈ N_D − N_A, with p = n_i²/n.

concepts.plainText: n = (ND - NA)/2 + sqrt( ((ND - NA)/2)^2 + ni^2 ),  then p = ni^2 / n

concepts.text: A doped sample passes through three temperature regions. At very low temperature (freeze-out) the dopant electrons are not ionised and conductivity is tiny. Over a wide middle range, which includes room temperature, the dopants are fully ionised and the majority concentration stays close to the doping level: this is the extrinsic region where devices are designed to work. At high temperature n_i, which rises steeply as T^(3/2) e^(−E_g/2kT) and roughly doubles for every 10 °C near room temperature in silicon, overtakes the doping and the sample behaves as intrinsic material. The larger band gap of silicon pushes this limit far above that of germanium.

concepts.plainText: Jn = q n mu_n E + q Dn dn/dx;   D / mu = kT/q = VT (Einstein relation)

concepts.text: The total current of each carrier type is the sum of a drift term driven by the field and a diffusion term driven by the concentration gradient. For holes the diffusion term carries a minus sign, because holes diffusing towards +x are a positive current towards +x while dp/dx is negative. The Einstein relation links the two mechanisms: both are limited by the same collisions, so D = μV_T, about 35 cm²/s for electrons in silicon. Injected minority carriers diffuse an average distance L = √(Dτ) before recombining, where τ is the carrier lifetime.

Worked example 1: resistance of a p-type silicon bar
Given: N_A = 10^16 per cm³, mu_p = 480 cm²/V·s, q = 1.6e-19 C
       length 5 mm, cross-section 0.5 mm x 0.5 mm
sigma = q N_A mu_p = 1.6e-19 x 1e16 x 480 = 0.768 S/cm
rho   = 1 / 0.768 = 1.30 ohm·cm
L = 0.5 cm, A = 0.05 cm x 0.05 cm = 2.5e-3 cm²
R = rho L / A = 1.30 x 0.5 / 2.5e-3 = 260 ohm
Minority electrons: n = (1.5e10)² / 1e16 = 2.25e4 per cm³
(so ignoring electrons in sigma is fully justified)

Worked example 2: compensated silicon
Given: N_D = 5e16, N_A = 2e16 per cm³, n_i = 1.5e10, kT = 0.026 eV
Net doping N_D - N_A = 3e16 >> n_i, so the sample is n-type
n = 3e16 per cm³,  p = (1.5e10)² / 3e16 = 7.5e3 per cm³
E_F - E_i = kT ln(n / n_i) = 0.026 x ln(2e6) = 0.026 x 14.5 = 0.377 eV
sigma ~ q n mu_n = 1.6e-19 x 3e16 x 1350 = 6.5 S/cm
Note: all 7e16 ions scatter carriers, so the real mobility,
and hence sigma, is lower than this lightly-doped estimate.
Common mistakes in carrier calculations:
items: Writing p = n_i/N_D instead of p = n_i²/N_D; the mass-action law uses n_i squared.
Mixing centimetres and metres: with μ in cm²/V·s and concentrations per cm³, lengths must be in cm (1 µm = 10^-4 cm) and σ comes out in S/cm.
Using the donor density alone in compensated material; the majority concentration is the net doping |N_D − N_A|.
Using μ_n for p-type majority conduction; holes are about three times less mobile in silicon.
Adding the minority term to σ in doped material; it is many orders of magnitude smaller and can be dropped.

concepts.text: The mobilities in the table are for lightly doped material at 300 K. Mobility falls as temperature rises (more lattice scattering) and as doping rises (more impurity scattering), so heavily doped regions conduct less well than a simple q N μ estimate predicts.

Checklist for any concentration question: find the net doping, set the majority concentration equal to it, get the minority concentration from n_i² divided by the majority value, and use only the majority term in σ = q N μ. Confirm the product n·p equals n_i² before choosing an option.

formulas.plainText: sigma = q (n mu_n + p mu_p);   rho = 1 / sigma
vd = mu x E;   J = sigma x E   (drift)
ni is proportional to T^(3/2) e^(-Eg/(2kT))

notes.text: Pentavalent = donor = n-type = electrons majority; trivalent = acceptor = p-type = holes majority. Memorise the dopant lists: P, As, Sb for n-type and B, Al, Ga, In for p-type.
A doped semiconductor is still electrically neutral. Having electrons as majority carriers does not make n-type material negatively charged; the fixed positive donor ions balance them exactly.

Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance: heating creates more electron-hole pairs, so resistance falls. Metals behave the opposite way, because heating only increases lattice scattering.
When a question gives n_i and a doping density, use n·p = n_i². For silicon with N_D = 10^16 per cm³, p = (1.5 × 10^10)² / 10^16 ≈ 2.25 × 10^4 per cm³.

formulas.title: Mass-Action Law
formulas.description: n and p are the electron and hole concentrations and ni the intrinsic concentration (1.5 × 10^10 per cm³ for Si at 300 K); holds in thermal equilibrium for any doping.

formulas.title: Majority and Minority Concentrations
formulas.description: For n-type material with donor density ND much larger than ni; for p-type swap the roles using the acceptor density NA.

formulas.title: Semiconductor Conductivity
formulas.description: q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C; mu_n and mu_p are the electron and hole mobilities; resistivity is rho = 1/sigma.

formulas.title: Drift Velocity
formulas.description: Average carrier velocity in an electric field E; the mobility mu is in cm²/(V·s) or m²/(V·s).

flashcards.front: Why does the resistance of a semiconductor fall when it is heated?
flashcards.back: Thermal energy breaks more covalent bonds and generates extra electron-hole pairs; more carriers mean lower resistance, a negative temperature coefficient.

flashcards.front: Band gap of silicon and germanium at room temperature?
flashcards.back: Silicon about 1.1 eV, germanium about 0.72 eV. The larger gap of silicon gives far lower leakage current and a higher permissible junction temperature.

flashcards.front: State the mass-action law.
flashcards.back: In thermal equilibrium n × p = n_i², so doping that increases the majority carriers reduces the minority carriers by the same factor.

flashcards.front: Name three donor and three acceptor impurities for silicon.
flashcards.back: Donors (pentavalent, n-type): phosphorus, arsenic, antimony. Acceptors (trivalent, p-type): boron, aluminium, gallium, indium.

questions.questionText: At absolute zero temperature, a pure silicon crystal behaves as:
questions.explanation: At 0 K every valence electron is locked in a covalent bond and the conduction band is empty, so no carriers are available and pure silicon acts as an insulator. Carriers appear only when thermal energy breaks bonds.

questions.questionText: Silicon is doped with 10^15 donor atoms per cm³. Taking n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, the equilibrium hole concentration is approximately:
questions.explanation: With n ≈ N_D = 10^15 per cm³, the mass-action law gives p = n_i²/n = (1.5 × 10^10)²/10^15 = 2.25 × 10^20/10^15 = 2.25 × 10^5 per cm³.

questions.questionText: Which impurity, when added to pure silicon, produces an n-type semiconductor?
questions.explanation: Arsenic is pentavalent and donates its fifth valence electron to the conduction band. Boron, gallium and aluminium are trivalent acceptors that give p-type material.

questions.questionText: Silicon is doped with 5 × 10^16 acceptor atoms per cm³. Taking n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, the equilibrium electron concentration is:
questions.explanation: p ≈ N_A = 5 × 10^16 per cm³, so n = n_i²/p = 2.25 × 10^20/(5 × 10^16) = 4.5 × 10^3 per cm³. Using n_i instead of n_i² gives the absurd 3 × 10^-7.

questions.questionText: In a semiconductor, a hole is best described as:
options: A vacancy left in a covalent bond, which behaves as a mobile positive charge
A positively charged nucleus that has lost all its electrons
A free proton moving through the crystal
A missing atom in the crystal lattice
questions.explanation: When a valence electron leaves a bond, the vacancy can be filled by a neighbouring bond electron, so the vacancy moves through the crystal and acts as a carrier of charge +q. No atom or proton moves.

questions.questionText: Using q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s and μ_p = 480 cm²/V·s, the resistivity of intrinsic silicon is about:
An n-type silicon sample has far more free electrons than holes. Its net electric charge is:
options: Negative, because electrons are the majority carriers
Zero, because the fixed positive donor ions balance the free electrons
Positive, because each donor atom has lost an electron
Negative at low temperature and positive at high temperature
questions.explanation: Every free electron from a donor leaves behind a fixed positive donor ion, and thermally generated pairs are also neutral, so the sample as a whole is neutral.

questions.questionText: n-type silicon has N_D = 10^16 per cm³. With q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C and μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s (ignore the holes), its resistivity is about:
questions.explanation: σ = q N_D μ_n = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 10^16 × 1350 = 2.16 S/cm, so ρ = 1/2.16 = 0.463 Ω·cm. The value 2.16 is σ, not ρ; using μ_p gives 1.30 Ω·cm.

questions.questionText: Arranged in order of increasing band gap at 300 K, the semiconductors germanium, silicon and gallium arsenide are:
questions.explanation: The band gaps are about 0.72 eV (Ge), 1.1 eV (Si) and 1.42 eV (GaAs).

questions.questionText: A bar of n-type silicon is 2 mm long with a 1 mm × 1 mm cross-section and N_D = 10^15 per cm³. With q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C and μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s, its resistance is about:
In an n-type semiconductor, the minority carriers (holes) arise mainly from:
options: Holes injected from the metal contacts
Ionisation of the donor atoms by the applied field
questions.explanation: Donors supply only electrons; every hole in n-type material comes from a thermally broken bond, which is why the minority concentration rises steeply with temperature.

questions.questionText: Electrons in silicon (μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s) are subjected to an electric field of 100 V/cm. Their drift velocity is:
questions.explanation: v_d = μE = 1350 × 100 = 1.35 × 10^5 cm/s = 1.35 × 10^3 m/s. Quoting 1.35 × 10^5 in m/s forgets the cm-to-m conversion; 4.8 × 10^2 m/s would be the hole value.

questions.questionText: Silicon has 5 × 10^22 atoms per cm³. It is doped with one donor atom per 10^8 silicon atoms. With n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, the hole concentration is:
questions.explanation: N_D = 5 × 10^22/10^8 = 5 × 10^14 per cm³ ≈ n, so p = n_i²/n = 2.25 × 10^20/(5 × 10^14) = 4.5 × 10^5 per cm³. The value 5 × 10^14 is the electron concentration.

questions.questionText: An n-type silicon sample with N_D = 10^16 per cm³ is warmed from 300 K to 350 K, still well within the extrinsic range. Which statement is correct?
options: The hole concentration rises greatly while the electron concentration stays almost equal to N_D
Both carrier concentrations stay exactly constant
The electron concentration doubles and the hole concentration halves
questions.explanation: n_i rises steeply with temperature, so the minority concentration p = n_i²/N_D increases by orders of magnitude. The majority concentration is fixed by the fully ionised donors as long as n_i remains much smaller than N_D.

questions.questionText: Silicon (n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³) is doped with N_D = 10^17 per cm³. By what factor is the hole concentration reduced below its intrinsic value?
Which statement about the mass-action law n·p = n_i² is NOT correct?
options: It applies only to intrinsic semiconductors
It holds in thermal equilibrium for both intrinsic and extrinsic material
Because n_i depends on temperature, the product n·p changes with temperature
Increasing the donor density lowers the hole density
questions.explanation: The law holds for any non-degenerate semiconductor in thermal equilibrium, doped or not; that is exactly what lets us find minority concentrations in extrinsic material.

questions.questionText: A silicon sample contains N_D = 3 × 10^16 donors and N_A = 10^16 acceptors per cm³. With n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, the type of the material and its hole concentration are:
questions.explanation: Net doping N_D − N_A = 2 × 10^16 per cm³ of donors, so it is n-type with n = 2 × 10^16 and p = 2.25 × 10^20/(2 × 10^16) ≈ 1.1 × 10^4 per cm³. Ignoring the acceptors gives 7.5 × 10^3.

questions.questionText: Diffusion current in a semiconductor is caused by:
options: Collisions of carriers with impurity ions
questions.explanation: Carriers move from regions of high concentration to low concentration by random thermal motion, even with no field. Current driven by an electric field is drift current.

questions.questionText: By what factor does the conductivity of silicon increase when it is doped with N_D = 10^16 per cm³, compared with intrinsic silicon? Use n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, μ_n = 1350 and μ_p = 480 cm²/V·s, and neglect holes in the doped sample.
questions.explanation: σ_doped/σ_i = N_D μ_n/[n_i(μ_n + μ_p)] = (10^16 × 1350)/(1.5 × 10^10 × 1830) ≈ 4.9 × 10^5. The ratio N_D/n_i = 6.7 × 10^5 alone ignores the mobilities.

questions.questionText: In silicon the electron mobility (about 1350 cm²/V·s) is greater than the hole mobility (about 480 cm²/V·s) mainly because:
options: Electrons carry a larger charge than holes
There are always more electrons than holes
Conduction-band electrons have a smaller effective mass and move more freely than holes, whose motion is a chain of valence-bond transfers
The applied field acts only on electrons
questions.explanation: Mobility depends on effective mass and scattering, not on concentration. Electrons and holes carry equal and opposite charge, and the field acts on both.

questions.questionText: What donor concentration gives n-type silicon a resistivity of 1 Ω·cm? Use q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C and μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s.
Which change would INCREASE the electron mobility in a silicon sample?
options: Reducing the doping concentration at the same temperature
questions.explanation: Mobility is limited by lattice scattering, which grows with temperature, and by impurity scattering, which grows with doping. Lighter doping therefore raises mobility; the applied voltage changes the drift velocity, not the mobility (at high fields mobility actually falls).

questions.questionText: At 300 K (V_T = kT/q = 26 mV), the diffusion constant of electrons in silicon with μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s is about:
questions.explanation: Einstein relation: D_n = μ_n V_T = 1350 × 0.026 = 35.1 cm²/s. Dividing μ by V_T gives 5.2 × 10^4; using μ_p = 480 gives 12.5 cm²/s.

questions.questionText: In an intrinsic semiconductor the Fermi level lies:
options: Very close to the middle of the band gap
questions.explanation: With equal electron and hole concentrations the Fermi level sits almost at mid-gap (exactly at mid-gap if the effective masses were equal). Donor doping moves it up towards the conduction band, acceptor doping down towards the valence band.

questions.questionText: The electron concentration in a silicon region falls linearly from 10^15 per cm³ to zero over a distance of 10 µm. With D_n = 35 cm²/s and q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, the magnitude of the electron diffusion current density is:
questions.explanation: dn/dx = 10^15/(10 × 10^-4 cm) = 10^18 per cm⁴; J = q D_n dn/dx = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 35 × 10^18 = 5.6 A/cm². Converting 10 µm wrongly as 10^-2 cm gives 0.56 A/cm².

questions.questionText: In n-type silicon, the donor energy level lies:
options: Slightly above the top of the valence band
Slightly below the bottom of the conduction band (roughly 0.05 eV)
Exactly at the middle of the band gap
questions.explanation: The fifth electron of a donor is so weakly bound that only a few hundredths of an electronvolt lift it into the conduction band, so donors are fully ionised at room temperature. Acceptor levels lie just above the valence band.

questions.questionText: For silicon (E_g = 1.1 eV, k = 8.62 × 10^-5 eV/K), using n_i ∝ T^(3/2) e^(−E_g/2kT), the ratio n_i(310 K)/n_i(300 K) is about:
questions.explanation: Ratio = (310/300)^1.5 × exp[(1.1/(2 × 8.62 × 10^-5)) × (1/300 − 1/310)] = 1.05 × e^0.686 ≈ 1.05 × 1.99 ≈ 2.1. Omitting the 2 in 2kT gives about 4.1; the temperature factor alone is only 1.05.

questions.questionText: Silicon has atomic number 14. The number of valence electrons in each silicon atom is:
questions.explanation: The configuration is 2, 8, 4, so silicon is tetravalent and forms four covalent bonds with its neighbours.

questions.questionText: Silicon's band gap is 1.1 eV. Expressed in joules (1 eV = 1.6 × 10^-19 J), this is:
questions.explanation: E = 1.1 × 1.6 × 10^-19 = 1.76 × 10^-19 J. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 6.9 × 10^18, which is absurdly large.

questions.questionText: Silicon is a poor light emitter, whereas GaAs is used in LEDs and laser diodes. The reason is that:
options: Silicon has an indirect band gap, while GaAs has a direct band gap
Silicon has a larger band gap than GaAs
GaAs cannot be doped n-type or p-type
Silicon has no holes at room temperature
questions.explanation: In a direct-gap material an electron can drop into a hole and emit a photon directly; in indirect-gap silicon the transition needs a lattice vibration as well, so recombination mostly produces heat. GaAs (1.42 eV) actually has the larger gap.

questions.questionText: The longest wavelength of light that can create electron-hole pairs in germanium (E_g = 0.72 eV) is about (use λ in µm ≈ 1.24/E_g in eV):
questions.explanation: λ_c = 1.24/0.72 = 1.72 µm; longer wavelengths carry photons of less than 0.72 eV. The value 1.13 µm is the silicon cut-off and 0.58 comes from inverting the ratio.

questions.questionText: The carrier lifetime in a semiconductor is the:
options: Average time an excess minority carrier exists before recombining
Time taken for a carrier to cross the whole device
Time needed to dope the crystal
Time after which the crystal becomes intrinsic
questions.explanation: Excess minority carriers recombine with majority carriers; their average survival time τ is the lifetime, and together with the diffusion constant it sets the diffusion length L = √(Dτ).

questions.questionText: Intrinsic silicon at 300 K has n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³. The total concentration of free carriers (electrons plus holes) is:
questions.explanation: In intrinsic material n = p = n_i, so n + p = 2 × 1.5 × 10^10 = 3 × 10^10 per cm³. 2.25 × 10^20 is the product n·p, not the sum.

questions.questionText: The Einstein relation connects which two carrier properties?
options: The conductivity and the resistivity: σ = 1/ρ
The diffusion constant and the mobility: D/μ = kT/q
The drift velocity and the field: v_d = μE
The electron and hole concentrations: n·p = n_i²
questions.explanation: Diffusion and drift are both limited by the same scattering processes, so D/μ equals the thermal voltage kT/q, about 26 mV at 300 K.

questions.questionText: Silicon contains 5 × 10^22 atoms per cm³. If it is doped with 10^16 donor atoms per cm³, there is one donor atom for every:
questions.explanation: 5 × 10^22/10^16 = 5 × 10^6, so one donor per five million silicon atoms. The inverse, 2 × 10^-7, is the fractional impurity content.

questions.questionText: A silicon sample is doped with N_D = N_A = 10^16 per cm³. Compared with pure silicon at the same temperature, this fully compensated sample has:
options: Electron and hole concentrations of 10^16 per cm³ each
About the same electron and hole concentrations (n ≈ p ≈ n_i), but lower mobility because of the ionised impurities
An electron concentration of 2 × 10^16 per cm³
questions.explanation: The acceptors capture all the donor electrons, so the net doping is zero and the mass-action law with neutrality gives n = p = n_i. The 2 × 10^16 ionised impurities still scatter carriers, lowering the mobility.

questions.questionText: Carriers in a semiconductor move with an average drift velocity of 2 × 10^4 cm/s in a field of 50 V/cm. Their mobility is:
questions.explanation: μ = v_d/E = 2 × 10^4/50 = 400 cm²/V·s. Multiplying gives 10^6 and inverting gives 2.5 × 10^-3.

questions.questionText: In an intrinsic semiconductor at room temperature:
options: There are more holes than free electrons
There are no holes, only free electrons
The free-electron concentration equals the hole concentration
questions.explanation: Each broken bond creates one free electron and one hole, so n = p = n_i. The conductivity is small but not zero at room temperature.

questions.questionText: p-type silicon has N_A = 2 × 10^16 per cm³ and μ_p = 480 cm²/V·s. With q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C and ignoring electrons, its conductivity is about:
questions.explanation: σ = q N_A μ_p = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 2 × 10^16 × 480 = 1.54 S/cm. Using μ_n = 1350 gives 4.32 S/cm, and 0.65 is the resistivity in Ω·cm.

questions.questionText: When an electric field is applied to a semiconductor, holes drift:
options: Opposite to the field, so their current cancels the electron current
In the direction of the field, but their current opposes the electron current
Not at all, because holes are fixed in the lattice
In the direction of the field, and their current adds to the electron current
questions.explanation: Holes are positive and move along the field, electrons move against it; because the charges are opposite, both motions give conventional current in the field direction, so σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p).

questions.questionText: An intrinsic germanium bar (n_i = 2.5 × 10^13 per cm³, μ_n = 3900 cm²/V·s, μ_p = 1900 cm²/V·s, q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C) has a field of 10 V/cm applied. The total drift current density is about:
questions.explanation: J = q n_i (μ_n + μ_p) E = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 2.5 × 10^13 × 5800 × 10 = 0.232 A/cm². Only the electron term gives 0.156 A/cm²; subtracting the mobilities gives 0.080 A/cm².

questions.questionText: If an extrinsic silicon sample is heated to a very high temperature (several hundred °C), it:
options: Behaves like intrinsic material, because thermally generated carriers far outnumber the dopant carriers
Changes permanently from n-type to p-type
Keeps its carrier concentration fixed at the doping level
questions.explanation: n_i grows exponentially with temperature; once it greatly exceeds the doping, n ≈ p ≈ n_i and the doping no longer controls conduction. This sets the upper temperature limit of devices.

questions.questionText: Using n_i = 2.5 × 10^13 per cm³ for Ge and 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³ for Si, and μ_n + μ_p = 5800 cm²/V·s for Ge and 1830 cm²/V·s for Si, the ratio of the intrinsic conductivity of germanium to that of silicon is about:
questions.explanation: σ_Ge/σ_Si = (2.5 × 10^13 × 5800)/(1.5 × 10^10 × 1830) ≈ 5.3 × 10^3. The n_i ratio alone is 1.7 × 10^3 and the mobility ratio alone is 3.2.

questions.questionText: The SI unit of carrier mobility μ is:
questions.explanation: Mobility is drift velocity per unit field, μ = v_d/E, so its unit is (m/s)/(V/m) = m²/(V·s). In practice it is usually quoted in cm²/(V·s), where 1 m²/(V·s) = 10^4 cm²/(V·s).

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a semiconductor?
questions.explanation: Copper is a metal whose conduction and valence bands overlap. Germanium, gallium arsenide and silicon carbide all have band gaps (about 0.72, 1.42 and 3.3 eV).

questions.questionText: In a silicon sample at 300 K (n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³) the measured hole concentration is 4 × 10^5 per cm³. The sample is:
options: p-type, with holes as majority carriers at 4 × 10^5 per cm³
questions.explanation: p is far below n_i, so holes are the minority carriers and the sample is n-type: n = n_i²/p = 2.25 × 10^20/(4 × 10^5) ≈ 5.6 × 10^14 per cm³.

questions.questionText: For n-type silicon with N_D = 10^16 per cm³ at 300 K (kT = 0.026 eV, n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³), how far above the intrinsic level E_i does the Fermi level lie? Use E_F − E_i = kT ln(N_D/n_i).
Excess electrons in p-type silicon have D_n = 35 cm²/s and lifetime τ_n = 1 µs. Their diffusion length L_n = √(D_n τ_n) is about:
questions.explanation: L_n = √(35 × 10^-6) cm = 5.92 × 10^-3 cm = 59 µm. Slipping a factor of 10 in the cm-to-µm conversion gives 5.9 or 590 µm.

subtopics.title: Semiconductor Diode
subtopics.subtitle: pn junction, bias behaviour, V-I curve, Shockley equation and special-purpose diodes

concepts.text: The P-N Junction

A diode is formed by joining p-type and n-type semiconductor in a single crystal. Majority carriers diffuse across the junction and recombine, leaving a thin depletion region of fixed ionised atoms with no free carriers. The uncovered charge sets up an electric field, and the resulting built-in barrier potential (about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium) stops further diffusion. The p side is the anode and the n side the cathode, marked by the band on the package.
Bias behaviour:
items: Forward bias (p to positive, n to negative): the barrier narrows, resistance is low and current flows freely once the applied voltage exceeds the knee voltage.
Reverse bias (p to negative, n to positive): the barrier widens, resistance is very high and only a tiny leakage (reverse saturation) current of minority carriers flows.
Excessive reverse voltage causes breakdown by the avalanche or Zener mechanism. This is destructive for a rectifier diode but is the normal working region of a Zener diode.

concepts.text: V-I Characteristic

The forward curve stays near zero until the knee (cut-in) voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium, then rises steeply and almost exponentially; the dynamic resistance r_d = nV_T/I_D is only a few ohms at milliampere currents. In reverse the current is the nearly constant saturation current I_S, of the order of nanoamperes for silicon and microamperes for germanium, until the breakdown voltage where it increases sharply. I_S roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature, and the forward drop falls by about 2 mV per °C.
Diode Current Equation
The ideal diode (Shockley) equation models current through the junction as a function of applied voltage. A single expression covers both forward and reverse bias:

concepts.plainText: ID = IS (e^(VD/(n VT)) - 1)

concepts.text: I_S is the reverse saturation current, V_T the thermal voltage (about 26 mV at room temperature), and n the ideality factor (1 to 2). For forward voltages above a few tenths of a volt the −1 is negligible and the current grows exponentially with V_D. For reverse voltages the exponential vanishes and I_D ≈ −I_S.
Diode Models

rows: Quick estimates, supply much larger than 0.7 V
Fixed drop of 0.7 V (Si) or 0.3 V (Ge)
Knee voltage in series with r_f (a few ohms)

concepts.text: Special Diodes

rows: AC to DC conversion, power supplies

concepts.text: An LED emits light when injected carriers recombine across a direct band gap (GaAs, GaP, GaN); its forward drop is 1.8 to 3.5 V depending on colour. A photodiode is reverse biased so that light-generated pairs in the depletion region produce a current proportional to illumination. A Schottky diode uses a metal-semiconductor junction with no minority-carrier storage, giving negligible reverse recovery time. A varactor exploits the fall of depletion-layer capacitance with increasing reverse voltage, and a tunnel diode is so heavily doped that quantum tunnelling gives a negative-resistance region in the forward characteristic.
Applications
Where diodes earn their keep in real circuits:
items: Rectification: a half-wave rectifier uses one diode; a full-wave rectifier uses a centre-tapped pair or a four-diode bridge, converting AC to pulsating DC.
Clipping and clamping: a diode with a reference voltage removes part of a waveform (clipper) or shifts its DC level (clamper).
Zener regulation: a Zener in reverse breakdown with a series resistor holds a nearly constant output voltage as the load or supply varies.
Freewheeling (flyback) diode: connected across an inductive load, it gives the stored energy a path when the switch opens and protects the switch from voltage spikes.
Signal work and protection: Schottky and fast diodes for demodulation, reverse-polarity protection and ESD clamping.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Diode Circuits and Calculations

Taking the logarithm of the forward Shockley equation gives V_D = nV_T ln(I_D/I_S). Two operating points of the same diode therefore differ in voltage by nV_T times the natural log of their current ratio, and I_S cancels out. With n = 1 and V_T = 26 mV a tenfold rise in current needs only about 60 mV more, and doubling the current needs about 18 mV. This is why the forward drop of a conducting silicon diode stays close to 0.6 to 0.8 V over several decades of current, which justifies the constant-voltage model.

concepts.plainText: V2 - V1 = n VT ln(I2/I1)   (about 60 mV per decade for n = 1)

concepts.text: Two kinds of resistance describe a diode. The static or DC resistance R_D = V_D/I_D is the ratio at one operating point and is tens to hundreds of ohms. The dynamic (AC) resistance r_d = nV_T/I_D is the slope of the curve at that point, is only a few ohms at milliampere currents, and is the one used for small signals superimposed on a DC bias. The operating point itself is where the diode curve meets the load line I_D = (V_S − V_D)/R drawn from V_S/R on the current axis to V_S on the voltage axis.

Worked example 1: diode current and resistances
Given: 5 V source, 1 kΩ series resistor, silicon diode (0.7 V), n = 1, V_T = 26 mV
Step 1  I_D = (5 − 0.7) / 1 kΩ = 4.3 mA
Step 2  Static resistance R_D = 0.7 V / 4.3 mA ≈ 163 Ω
Step 3  Dynamic resistance r_d = 26 mV / 4.3 mA ≈ 6.0 Ω
Step 4  Raising I_D to 43 mA would raise V_D by only 26 mV × ln 10 ≈ 60 mV

concepts.plainText: Vr(pp) ~ Idc / (fr C), fr = f (half-wave) or 2f (full-wave)

Worked example 2: bridge rectifier with capacitor filter
Given: 12 V rms secondary, 50 Hz, silicon bridge, load 100 mA, C = 1000 µF
Step 1  V_m = 12 × √2 = 16.97 V
Step 2  Two diodes conduct in series: V_m(out) = 16.97 − 1.4 = 15.57 V
Step 3  Without the capacitor: V_dc = 2 × 15.57 / π = 9.91 V
Step 4  Ripple frequency f_r = 2 × 50 = 100 Hz
Step 5  With the capacitor: V_r(pp) = 0.1 / (100 × 1000 µF) = 1.0 V
Step 6  V_dc ≈ 15.57 − 1.0/2 ≈ 15.1 V

A clipper removes the part of a waveform beyond a set level: a shunt diode in series with a battery V_B starts conducting when the output reaches V_B plus the diode drop, so the output is held there. A clamper uses a series capacitor and a shunt diode. On the first peak the capacitor charges to the peak voltage minus the diode drop, and afterwards it acts as a battery that shifts the whole waveform up or down without changing its peak-to-peak value. The RC time constant must be much longer than the signal period so the capacitor does not discharge between peaks.

Worked example 3: Zener regulator design and check
Given: V_in = 12 V, V_Z = 6 V, load 20 mA, desired I_Z = 10 mA
Step 1  I_R = I_Z + I_L = 10 + 20 = 30 mA
Step 2  R_S = (12 − 6) / 30 mA = 200 Ω
Step 3  Load removed: I_Z = 30 mA, P_Z = 6 V × 30 mA = 180 mW
Step 4  Choose a Zener rated well above 180 mW (e.g. 400 mW)
Common mistakes in diode problems:
items: Forgetting that a bridge has two diode drops in the conducting path while a centre-tapped rectifier has one.
Using the rms value where the peak is needed: V_m = √2 × V_rms.
Assuming a Zener regulates before checking that the open-circuit voltage across it exceeds V_Z.
Mixing up PIV: 2V_m for the centre-tapped circuit, V_m for the bridge and half-wave circuits.
Using the static resistance V_D/I_D in a small-signal problem, where the dynamic resistance nV_T/I_D is required.

concepts.text: When two diodes of different material are in parallel, the one with the lower knee voltage (germanium, 0.3 V) turns on first and clamps the voltage, so the silicon diode never reaches 0.7 V and carries no current.

formulas.plainText: ID ~ IS e^(VD/nVT)   for VD >> VT (forward)
IR = (Vin - VZ) / RS = IZ + IL   (Zener regulator)

notes.text: Remember the pair 0.7 V (Si) / 0.3 V (Ge). For circuit analysis with an ideal diode assume 0 V drop; with the practical model use the knee voltage.
A Zener diode regulates because the voltage across it stays nearly constant over a wide range of reverse current.
Reverse saturation current is a minority-carrier current: it depends strongly on temperature (roughly doubling every 10 °C) but hardly at all on the reverse voltage until breakdown.
The operating region of special diodes is a common MCQ: photodiode, varactor and Zener work in reverse bias (the Zener in breakdown); LED, Schottky and tunnel diodes work in forward bias.

formulas.description: IS is the reverse saturation current, VT the thermal voltage (26 mV at 300 K) and n the ideality factor (1 to 2); gives the full forward and reverse V-I curve.

formulas.title: Thermal Voltage
formulas.plainText: VT = kT / q ~ 26 mV at 300 K
formulas.description: k = 1.38 × 10^-23 J/K, q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, T in kelvin; about 26 mV at room temperature.

formulas.title: Diode Dynamic Resistance
