flashcards.front: What is the reverse saturation current of a diode and what does it depend on?
flashcards.back: The small minority-carrier current in reverse bias (nanoamperes for Si, microamperes for Ge). It is almost independent of reverse voltage but roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise.

flashcards.front: Which special diodes are operated in reverse bias?
flashcards.back: Zener (in reverse breakdown), photodiode and varactor. LED, Schottky and tunnel diodes are forward biased in normal use.

flashcards.front: Why is a Schottky diode faster than an ordinary pn diode?
flashcards.back: It is a metal-semiconductor junction with no minority-carrier storage, so it has negligible reverse recovery time and a low forward drop of 0.2 to 0.3 V.

questions.questionText: The depletion region of an unbiased pn junction consists mainly of:
options: A high concentration of free electrons and holes
Immobile ionised donor and acceptor atoms with almost no free carriers
Only free electrons that have diffused from the n side
Neutral atoms of the intrinsic semiconductor
questions.explanation: Majority carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving uncovered positive donor ions on the n side and negative acceptor ions on the p side; the region is depleted of mobile carriers.

questions.questionText: When the forward bias applied to a pn junction is increased, the width of the depletion region:
questions.explanation: Forward bias opposes the built-in potential, pushing majority carriers towards the junction and narrowing the depletion layer.

questions.questionText: For a silicon diode carrying a constant forward current, a rise in junction temperature causes its forward voltage to:
questions.explanation: Because I_S rises steeply with temperature, less voltage is needed for the same current; the forward drop has a temperature coefficient of about −2 mV/°C.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode (practical model, V_D = 0.7 V) is connected in forward bias in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 5 V DC supply. The diode current is:
questions.explanation: I = (5 − 0.7)/1 kΩ = 4.3 mA. Ignoring the drop gives 5 mA; using 0.3 V (germanium) gives 4.7 mA.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode has I_S = 1 × 10^-13 A and n = 1. Taking V_T = 26 mV, the forward current at V_D = 0.60 V is about:
For a diode with ideality factor n = 2 at V_T = 26 mV, the increase in forward voltage needed to raise the current tenfold is about:
questions.explanation: ΔV = nV_T ln(10) = 2 × 26 mV × 2.303 ≈ 120 mV. With n = 1 it would be about 60 mV.

questions.questionText: A diode (n = 1, V_T = 26 mV) has a forward drop of 0.650 V at 1 mA. Using the Shockley equation, its forward voltage at 20 mA is about:
The dynamic (AC) resistance of a forward-biased diode with n = 1 at I_D = 2 mA and V_T = 26 mV is:
questions.explanation: r_d = nV_T/I_D = 26 mV / 2 mA = 13 Ω.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode has a forward voltage of 0.65 V when it carries 5 mA. Its static (DC) resistance at this point is:
questions.explanation: R_D = V_D/I_D = 0.65 V / 5 mA = 130 Ω. The 5.2 Ω value is the dynamic resistance 26 mV/5 mA, which is a different quantity.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the dynamic resistance r_d of a forward-biased diode is correct?
options: It is equal to V_D/I_D at the operating point
It is inversely proportional to the DC current through the diode
It increases as the forward current increases
It is independent of the operating point
questions.explanation: r_d = nV_T/I_D is the slope of the V-I curve at the Q-point; doubling I_D halves r_d. V_D/I_D is the static resistance.

questions.questionText: A diode biased at I_D = 0.5 mA (n = 1, V_T = 25 mV) is fed a 10 mV peak AC signal through a 950 Ω series resistor, with the DC bias path having no effect on the AC signal. The peak AC voltage across the diode is:
questions.explanation: r_d = 25 mV / 0.5 mA = 50 Ω. By voltage division v_d = 10 mV × 50/(950 + 50) = 0.5 mV.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode (0.7 V) and a germanium diode (0.3 V) are connected in series, both forward biased, with a 2.2 kΩ resistor across a 12 V DC supply. The circuit current is:
A silicon diode is connected in reverse bias in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 10 V DC supply. Using the practical model, the voltage across the resistor is about:
questions.explanation: A reverse-biased diode behaves as an open circuit, so almost no current flows; the resistor drop is about 0 V and nearly all 10 V appears across the diode.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode (0.7 V) and a germanium diode (0.3 V) are connected in parallel, both forward biased, and fed from a 10 V DC supply through a 1 kΩ resistor. The current through the silicon diode is about:
questions.explanation: The germanium diode turns on first and holds the parallel voltage at 0.3 V, below the 0.7 V the silicon diode needs, so the silicon diode carries practically no current; the germanium diode carries (10 − 0.3)/1 k = 9.7 mA.

questions.questionText: Two identical silicon diodes (0.7 V) are connected in parallel and fed from a 5 V DC supply through a 430 Ω resistor. Assuming they share current equally, the current in each diode is:
questions.explanation: Total current = (5 − 0.7)/430 = 10 mA; shared equally, each diode carries 5.0 mA.

questions.questionText: A half-wave rectifier with an ideal diode is fed a sinusoidal voltage of 20 V peak. The average (DC) output voltage across a resistive load is:
questions.explanation: V_dc = V_m/π = 20/π = 6.37 V. The value 2V_m/π = 12.7 V applies to a full-wave rectifier.

questions.questionText: A bridge rectifier using silicon diodes (0.7 V each) is fed from a transformer secondary of 12 V rms and drives a resistive load with no filter. The average output voltage is about:
questions.explanation: V_m = 12√2 = 16.97 V; two diodes conduct, so the output peak is 16.97 − 1.4 = 15.57 V and V_dc = 2 × 15.57/π = 9.91 V.

questions.questionText: In a centre-tapped full-wave rectifier each half of the secondary delivers 15 V peak. With ideal diodes, the peak inverse voltage across each diode is:
questions.explanation: When one diode conducts, the non-conducting diode sees the full secondary: PIV = 2V_m = 2 × 15 = 30 V.

questions.questionText: For the same peak secondary voltage V_m per diode path, which rectifier requires diodes with a peak inverse voltage rating of 2V_m?
options: None; every rectifier requires only V_m
questions.explanation: In the centre-tapped circuit the reverse-biased diode sees the voltage of both halves of the secondary, 2V_m; in the bridge each diode sees only V_m.

questions.questionText: A full-wave rectifier is supplied from 50 Hz mains. The fundamental frequency of the ripple in its output is:
questions.explanation: A full-wave rectifier produces two output pulses per input cycle, so the ripple frequency is 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.

questions.questionText: The ripple factor of an unfiltered full-wave rectifier with a resistive load is about:
questions.explanation: γ = √((V_rms/V_dc)² − 1) with V_rms = V_m/√2 and V_dc = 2V_m/π gives √(π²/8 − 1) ≈ 0.48; the half-wave value is 1.21.

questions.questionText: The maximum theoretical rectification efficiency (DC load power divided by AC input power) of a half-wave rectifier is:
questions.explanation: η = P_dc/P_ac = (V_m/π)²/(V_m/2)² = 4/π² = 0.405, i.e. 40.5 %; a full-wave rectifier reaches 8/π² = 81.1 %.

questions.questionText: A full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz mains feeds a 100 mA load through a 1000 µF reservoir capacitor. The approximate peak-to-peak ripple voltage is:
questions.explanation: V_r(pp) = I/(f_r C) with f_r = 2 × 50 = 100 Hz: 0.1/(100 × 1000 × 10^-6) = 1.0 V. Using 50 Hz gives the half-wave value, 2.0 V.

questions.questionText: A half-wave rectifier with a silicon diode (0.7 V) is fed a 10 V peak sine wave and drives a 1 kΩ resistive load. The average load current is about:
questions.explanation: Peak current = (10 − 0.7)/1 kΩ = 9.3 mA; average for a half-wave = I_m/π = 9.3/π = 2.96 mA.

questions.questionText: In a shunt clipper, a silicon diode (0.7 V) in series with a 3 V battery is connected across the output, arranged so that it conducts when the output exceeds the battery voltage. A 10 V peak sine wave is applied through a series resistor. The positive peak of the output is:
questions.explanation: The diode conducts once the output reaches V_B + V_D = 3 + 0.7 = 3.7 V, so the positive peaks are clipped at 3.7 V.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes a clipper from a clamper?
options: A clipper shifts the DC level, while a clamper removes part of the waveform
Both remove part of the waveform, but a clamper needs a battery
A clamper needs no capacitor, while a clipper always needs one
A clipper removes part of the waveform, while a clamper shifts the DC level without changing the waveform's shape
questions.explanation: Clippers cut off the part of the signal beyond a reference level; clampers use a capacitor and diode to add a DC shift while keeping the peak-to-peak value.

questions.questionText: A ±5 V square wave is applied to an ideal-diode positive clamper (series capacitor, shunt diode), whose RC time constant is much longer than the period. The output swings between:
questions.explanation: The capacitor charges to 5 V during the negative half and then adds 5 V to the input, shifting the ±5 V wave up to 0 V to +10 V; peak-to-peak stays 10 V.

questions.questionText: A 10 V peak sine wave is applied to a clamper: a series capacitor followed by a silicon diode (0.7 V) whose anode is connected to the output and cathode to ground, with a long RC time constant. In the steady state, the output swings between about:
questions.explanation: On positive peaks the diode conducts and the capacitor charges to 10 − 0.7 = 9.3 V, so v_out = v_in − 9.3 V, which ranges from +0.7 V to −19.3 V.

questions.questionText: For a clamper circuit to keep the output waveform shape undistorted, its RC time constant should be:
options: Much smaller than the period of the input signal
Much larger than the period of the input signal
Exactly equal to half the period
Equal to the diode's reverse recovery time
questions.explanation: A long time constant (typically RC ≥ 5T or more) keeps the capacitor from discharging noticeably between peaks, so the shift stays constant.

questions.questionText: A two-level clipper has two silicon diodes (0.7 V) across the output: one in series with a +4 V battery that limits positive swings, and one in series with a 6 V battery that limits negative swings. A 10 V peak sine wave is applied through a series resistor. The output is limited to between about:
questions.explanation: Each branch conducts when the output exceeds its battery voltage plus 0.7 V: the positive peaks are clipped at 4 + 0.7 = 4.7 V and the negative peaks at −(6 + 0.7) = −6.7 V.

questions.questionText: Zener breakdown, as distinct from avalanche breakdown, is characterised by:
options: Lightly doped junctions, a breakdown voltage above about 6 V and a positive temperature coefficient
Carrier multiplication by impact ionisation in a wide depletion layer
Heavily doped junctions, a breakdown voltage below about 5 V and a negative temperature coefficient
questions.explanation: In heavily doped junctions the thin depletion layer lets the strong field pull electrons directly out of bonds (field emission) at low voltage; this breakdown voltage falls as temperature rises. Avalanche breakdown occurs in lightly doped junctions at higher voltage.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the temperature coefficient of Zener diodes is correct?
options: Diodes rated near 5 to 6 V have a temperature coefficient close to zero
All Zener diodes have a positive temperature coefficient
Low-voltage (below 4 V) Zeners have a positive temperature coefficient
The temperature coefficient is independent of the breakdown voltage
questions.explanation: Field-emission breakdown (low voltage) has a negative coefficient and avalanche breakdown (high voltage) a positive one; around 5 to 6 V the two effects nearly cancel.

questions.questionText: A Zener regulator has V_in = 20 V, series resistor R_S = 200 Ω, V_Z = 10 V and a 1 kΩ load. The Zener current is:

A Zener regulator has V_in = 15 V, R_S = 100 Ω and V_Z = 9 V. The Zener needs at least 5 mA to stay in regulation. The smallest load resistance that can be connected while keeping regulation is about:
questions.explanation: I_R = (15 − 9)/100 = 60 mA; maximum load current = 60 − 5 = 55 mA; R_L(min) = 9 V / 55 mA ≈ 164 Ω.

questions.questionText: A Zener regulator has V_in = 24 V, R_S = 120 Ω and V_Z = 12 V. If the load is disconnected, the power dissipated in the Zener diode is:
questions.explanation: With no load all the series current flows in the Zener: I_Z = (24 − 12)/120 = 100 mA, so P_Z = 12 V × 0.1 A = 1.2 W.

questions.questionText: A 6 V Zener regulator is fed from 12 V and must supply a 20 mA load while keeping 10 mA in the Zener. The required series resistance is:
An unloaded Zener regulator has R_S = 95 Ω and a Zener with dynamic resistance r_z = 5 Ω operating in breakdown. If the input voltage rises by 1 V, the output voltage rises by about:
questions.explanation: For changes the Zener acts as r_z, so ΔV_out = ΔV_in × r_z/(R_S + r_z) = 1 × 5/100 = 50 mV.

questions.questionText: A 10 V Zener diode is used in a regulator with V_in = 8 V, R_S = 1 kΩ and R_L = 1 kΩ. The output voltage is:
questions.explanation: With the Zener removed the load would see 8 × 1k/(1k + 1k) = 4 V, which is below V_Z, so the Zener stays off and the output is simply 4 V.

questions.questionText: The capacitance of a varactor diode decreases as the reverse bias is increased because:
options: The depletion region narrows, reducing the plate area
The depletion region widens, increasing the effective plate separation
Minority carriers are stored in the junction
The junction breaks down and conducts
questions.explanation: The depletion layer is the dielectric between two conducting regions; more reverse voltage widens it, so C = εA/W falls.

questions.questionText: An abrupt-junction varactor has C ∝ 1/√V_R (built-in potential neglected). If its capacitance is 40 pF at a reverse voltage of 4 V, its capacitance at 16 V is:
The dark current of a photodiode is:
options: The forward current at the knee voltage
The current produced by the maximum rated illumination
The current that flows during reverse breakdown
The small reverse current that flows when no light falls on it
questions.explanation: In reverse bias a photodiode carries only the thermally generated reverse saturation current in darkness; light adds a photocurrent proportional to illumination.

questions.questionText: The colour of light emitted by an LED is determined mainly by:
options: The magnitude of the forward current
The band-gap energy of the semiconductor material
The colour of the plastic package
The value of the series resistor
questions.explanation: Photon energy is roughly equal to the band gap, so λ ≈ hc/E_g; GaAs gives infrared, GaAsP red to yellow and GaN blue.

questions.questionText: Which statement about special-purpose diodes is NOT correct?
options: A tunnel diode is lightly doped so that its depletion region is very wide
A Schottky diode uses a metal-semiconductor junction
A varactor is operated in reverse bias as a voltage-variable capacitor
An LED emits light when carriers recombine under forward bias
questions.explanation: A tunnel diode is very heavily doped, giving an extremely thin depletion region through which electrons tunnel and a negative-resistance region; the other statements are correct.

questions.questionText: Which junction capacitance dominates in a pn diode under forward bias?
questions.explanation: Under forward bias the stored minority charge near the junction changes with voltage, giving a diffusion capacitance proportional to current; the transition capacitance of the depletion layer dominates in reverse bias.

subtopics.title: Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT)
subtopics.subtitle: npn and pnp structure, alpha and beta, CB/CE/CC configurations and operating regions

concepts.text: Bipolar Junction Transistor

A BJT has three terminals — emitter, base, collector — and two pn junctions. It is a current-controlled device: a small base current controls a much larger collector current. Two types exist: npn, with a thin p-type base between n-type emitter and collector, and pnp, with an n-type base between p-type emitter and collector. On the symbol the arrow sits on the emitter and shows the direction of conventional current: it points outward for npn and inward for pnp.
Structure and doping of the three regions:
items: Emitter: heavily doped and moderately sized, so that it injects a large number of carriers into the base.
Base: very thin and lightly doped, so that almost all injected carriers cross it without recombining and only a small fraction leaves through the base terminal.
Collector: lightly doped and the largest region, so that it collects the carriers and dissipates most of the heat; its junction has the higher breakdown voltage.
Because of these asymmetries the emitter and collector cannot be interchanged in practice, even though both are the same material type.

concepts.text: Operation and Current Relations

For amplification the emitter-base junction is forward biased (about 0.7 V for silicon) and the collector-base junction is reverse biased. In an npn device the forward-biased emitter injects electrons into the base; because the base is thin and lightly doped, more than 95 % of them diffuse across and are swept into the collector by the reverse-biased junction. The few that recombine, together with holes injected back into the emitter, form the small base current. The collector current is therefore almost independent of collector voltage and is set by the base current, or equivalently by V_BE.

concepts.plainText: IE = IC + IB
beta = IC/IB;   alpha = IC/IE = beta/(beta + 1)

concepts.text: Alpha (α, the common-base current gain) is always slightly less than 1, typically 0.95 to 0.995. Beta (β or h_FE, the common-emitter current gain) is typically 50 to 300 and varies with temperature, collector current and from one device to another of the same type. Because I_E = I_B + I_C, the two gains are linked by β = α/(1 − α) and α = β/(1 + β).

Worked example: if α = 0.99 then β = 0.99/(1 − 0.99) = 99. With I_E = 10 mA the base current is I_B = I_E/(1 + β) = 10/100 = 0.1 mA and I_C = βI_B = 9.9 mA. Going the other way, β = 200 gives α = 200/201 ≈ 0.995.
Operating Regions

As an amplifier the transistor is biased in the middle of the active region, typically with V_CE ≈ V_CC/2, so that the output can swing both ways without distortion. As a switch it is driven hard between cut-off (both junctions reverse biased, I_C ≈ 0) and saturation (both junctions forward biased, V_CE ≈ 0.1 to 0.3 V). In saturation the collector current is limited by the external circuit rather than by βI_B, so the base is overdriven with I_B greater than I_C(sat)/β.

Leakage currents: I_CBO is the collector-base reverse current measured with the emitter open; it is the reverse saturation current of the collector junction and roughly doubles every 10 °C. I_CEO, the collector-emitter current with the base open, is much larger because the leakage acts as base current and is amplified: I_CEO = (1 + β)I_CBO. Including leakage, I_C = βI_B + I_CEO, and this temperature-dependent term is the cause of thermal runaway in a poorly stabilised bias circuit.
Configurations
Configurations, named after the terminal common to input and output:
items: Common Base: current gain α < 1, high voltage gain, no phase shift, very low input impedance; used in high-frequency amplifiers.
Common Emitter: high current gain β AND high voltage gain, 180 degree phase shift — the standard amplifier stage.
Common Collector (emitter follower): current gain γ = 1 + β, voltage gain about 1, high input and low output impedance — used as a buffer and for impedance matching.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: BJT Biasing and the Q-Point

The relation β = α/(1 − α) follows directly from I_E = I_C + I_B. Dividing by I_C gives 1/α = 1 + 1/β, which rearranges to both standard forms. Because α is so close to 1, a tiny change in α makes a large change in β: α = 0.99 gives β = 99, while α = 0.995 gives β = 199. Including the collector leakage, the complete collector current is I_C = βI_B + (1 + β)I_CBO, and it is this leakage term, doubling roughly every 10 °C, that a bias circuit must keep under control.

Biasing sets the DC operating point, or Q-point (I_CQ, V_CEQ), about which the signal swings. For a common-emitter stage with collector resistor R_C and emitter resistor R_E, every possible DC operating point lies on the DC load line V_CE = V_CC − I_C(R_C + R_E). Its end points are I_C(sat) = V_CC/(R_C + R_E) on the current axis and V_CE(off) = V_CC on the voltage axis. The Q-point is where this line crosses the output characteristic for the actual base current; placing it near the middle allows the largest undistorted swing.

concepts.plainText: VCE = VCC - IC (RC + RE)   (DC load line, IE ~ IC)

Good: a rise in I_C lowers V_C and so I_B

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: fixed bias, check the region
Given: V_CC = 12 V, R_B = 470 kΩ, R_C = 2.2 kΩ, β = 100, V_BE = 0.7 V
Step 1  I_B = (12 − 0.7)/470 kΩ = 24.0 µA
Step 2  I_C = βI_B = 100 × 24.0 µA = 2.40 mA
Step 3  V_CE = 12 − 2.40 mA × 2.2 kΩ = 6.71 V
Step 4  V_CE > V_CE(sat) ≈ 0.2 V, so the transistor is active: Q = (2.40 mA, 6.71 V)
If β were 250: I_C would be 6.0 mA and V_CE = 12 − 13.2 < 0, impossible,
so the transistor saturates with I_C(sat) = (12 − 0.2)/2.2 kΩ ≈ 5.4 mA

Worked example 2: voltage-divider bias, exact and approximate
Given: V_CC = 18 V, R_1 = 82 kΩ, R_2 = 22 kΩ, R_E = 1.2 kΩ, β = 50, V_BE = 0.7 V
Step 1  V_TH = 18 × 22/104 = 3.81 V, R_TH = 82 × 22/104 = 17.3 kΩ
Step 2  Exact: I_B = (3.81 − 0.7)/(17.3 k + 51 × 1.2 k) = 39.6 µA
Step 3  I_C = 50 × 39.6 µA = 1.98 mA
Step 4  Approximate: V_E = 3.81 − 0.7 = 3.11 V, I_E = 3.11/1.2 k = 2.59 mA
Step 5  Check βR_E = 60 kΩ versus 10R_2 = 220 kΩ: condition fails,
        so the approximate method is not valid here; use the exact result

The stability factor S = ΔI_C/ΔI_CBO measures how much the collector current shifts when leakage rises with temperature. For fixed bias S = 1 + β, the worst case; the ideal value is 1. Adding R_E or feeding the base from the collector reduces S because any rise in I_C raises the emitter voltage, or lowers the collector voltage, and cuts the base drive. The voltage-divider circuit with a large R_E and a stiff divider (βR_E at least ten times R_2) gives S close to 1 and a Q-point almost independent of β.
Common mistakes in bias problems:
items: Forgetting the (β + 1) factor when referring R_E to the base circuit.
Calculating V_CE with I_C × R_C only, and leaving out the drop I_E × R_E.
Accepting a negative V_CE instead of recognising that the transistor has saturated.
Using the approximate voltage-divider method when βR_E is not at least 10R_2.
Treating the load-line saturation current as V_CC/R_C when an emitter resistor is present.

concepts.text: I_C = βI_B holds only in the active region. Always check the answer: if the calculated V_CE is below about 0.2 V, the transistor is saturated and the collector current is set by the external resistors, not by β.

For voltage-divider bias, first find V_B from the divider, then V_E = V_B − 0.7 V, I_E = V_E/R_E and finally V_CE = V_CC − I_C(R_C + R_E). This four-step route solves most Q-point problems in under a minute.

notes.text: Amplifier questions assume the ACTIVE region. Switching questions toggle between cut-off (OFF) and saturation (ON).

Beta is not a constant. It changes with temperature, collector current and between individual transistors of the same type, so good bias circuits (voltage-divider or emitter-stabilised) are designed to be insensitive to β.
The emitter arrow shows the direction of conventional current and always points from p to n: outward for npn (Not Pointing iN), inward for pnp.
Quick check: I_B/I_E = 1 − α = 1/(1 + β). A gain of β = 99 means exactly 1 % of the emitter current leaves through the base.

flashcards.front: Why is the base of a BJT made thin and lightly doped?
flashcards.back: So that nearly all carriers injected from the emitter cross to the collector without recombining, keeping I_B small and β large.

flashcards.front: Which BJT configuration has a voltage gain of about 1, and what is it used for?
flashcards.back: The common collector (emitter follower). Its high input and low output impedance make it a buffer and impedance-matching stage.

flashcards.front: How are I_CEO and I_CBO related?
flashcards.back: I_CEO = (1 + β) I_CBO. With the base open, the collector-base leakage acts as base current and is amplified.

questions.questionText: In an npn transistor operating in the active region, the current across the base region is carried mainly by:
options: Holes supplied by the base terminal
Electrons generated thermally in the collector
questions.explanation: The forward-biased emitter junction injects electrons into the thin p-type base, where they are minority carriers that diffuse across to the collector.

questions.questionText: In a BJT, the most heavily doped region is the:
questions.explanation: The emitter is heavily doped so that it injects a large number of carriers into the base; the base is lightly doped and the collector moderately to lightly doped.

questions.questionText: The region of a BJT that is physically the largest, so that it can dissipate most of the heat, is the:
questions.explanation: Most of the power V_CE × I_C is dissipated at the collector junction, so the collector is made the largest region.

questions.questionText: In a transistor, the emitter current is 5 mA and the collector current is 4.9 mA. The base current is:
A transistor has a common-emitter current gain β = 150. Its common-base current gain α is about:
questions.explanation: α = β/(1 + β) = 150/151 = 0.993. The value 1.007 comes from inverting the ratio; α can never exceed 1.

questions.questionText: A transistor with α = 0.99 is operated in the active region with a base current of 40 µA. The collector current is:
A transistor has β = 50 and a collector-base leakage current I_CBO = 10 µA. With a base current of 40 µA in the active region, the total collector current is:
As the collector-base reverse voltage of a BJT is increased, the effective base width decreases. This Early effect (base-width modulation) causes:
options: A decrease in β and in collector current
The emitter junction to become reverse biased
The collector current to become exactly independent of V_CE
A slight rise in I_C with V_CE, giving the output characteristics an upward slope
questions.explanation: The wider collector depletion layer eats into the base, so fewer carriers recombine; β and I_C rise slightly with V_CE, which gives the transistor a finite output resistance.

questions.questionText: The emitter follower is another name for which transistor configuration?
questions.explanation: In the common-collector stage the output is taken from the emitter and follows the base voltage less about 0.7 V, with a voltage gain close to 1.

questions.questionText: Which BJT configuration has the lowest input impedance?
questions.explanation: In the common-base stage the signal drives the emitter, which looks like the small resistance r_e (tens of ohms); the CC stage has the highest input impedance.

questions.questionText: In which BJT amplifier configuration is the output voltage 180° out of phase with the input voltage?
questions.explanation: In the CE stage a rise in base voltage increases I_C, increasing the drop across R_C and lowering the collector voltage, so the output is inverted; the CB and CC stages give no phase inversion.

questions.questionText: A transistor with β = 80 is used in the common-collector configuration. Its current gain (emitter current divided by base current) is:
questions.explanation: For the CC configuration the output is I_E, so the current gain is I_E/I_B = 1 + β = 81.

questions.questionText: For an npn silicon transistor, measurements give V_BE = 0.7 V and V_BC = 0.5 V. The transistor is operating in the:
questions.explanation: V_BE > 0 forward biases the emitter junction and V_BC > 0 forward biases the collector junction; both forward biased means saturation.

questions.questionText: A fixed-bias npn circuit has V_CC = 10 V, R_B = 100 kΩ, R_C = 2 kΩ and β = 100. Taking V_BE = 0.7 V and V_CE(sat) = 0.2 V, the actual collector current is:
questions.explanation: I_B = 9.3/100 k = 93 µA, so βI_B = 9.3 mA would need V_CE = 10 − 18.6 < 0; the transistor is saturated and I_C = (10 − 0.2)/2 kΩ = 4.9 mA.

questions.questionText: A fixed-bias silicon transistor circuit has V_CC = 12 V, R_B = 470 kΩ, R_C = 2.2 kΩ and β = 100 (V_BE = 0.7 V). The collector-emitter voltage V_CE is about:
A common-emitter stage has V_CC = 15 V, R_C = 3 kΩ and no emitter resistor. The saturation end of its DC load line (ideal, V_CE(sat) = 0) is at a collector current of:
questions.explanation: I_C(sat) = V_CC/R_C = 15/3 kΩ = 5 mA; the other end of the load line is V_CE = V_CC = 15 V.

questions.questionText: A transistor stage has V_CC = 12 V, R_C = 2 kΩ and R_E = 1 kΩ. Taking I_E ≈ I_C and V_CE(sat) = 0, the DC load line meets the current axis at:
questions.explanation: Both resistors carry the collector current, so I_C(sat) = V_CC/(R_C + R_E) = 12/3 kΩ = 4 mA.

The stability factor S = ΔI_C/ΔI_CBO of a fixed-bias (base-resistor) circuit is:
questions.explanation: In fixed bias I_B is set by R_B alone, so a change in I_CBO appears in I_C multiplied by (1 + β), the worst possible value; the ideal value is 1.

questions.questionText: Which biasing method gives the most stable Q-point against changes in β and temperature?
options: Voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor
Base bias with the emitter grounded
questions.explanation: With a stiff divider and R_E, V_B is fixed by the divider and I_E ≈ (V_B − V_BE)/R_E, which hardly depends on β.

questions.questionText: In a collector-feedback bias circuit, R_B = 100 kΩ is connected from collector to base, R_C = 1 kΩ, V_CC = 10 V, β = 100 and there is no emitter resistor (V_BE = 0.7 V). The collector current is about:
questions.explanation: R_C carries I_C + I_B = (β + 1)I_B, so 10 = 101 I_B × 1 k + I_B × 100 k + 0.7, giving I_B = 9.3/201 k = 46.3 µA and I_C = 100 × 46.3 µA = 4.63 mA.

questions.questionText: Collector-to-base (collector feedback) bias improves Q-point stability because:
options: It keeps the base voltage fixed by a resistor divider
It forces the transistor into saturation
It makes β independent of temperature
A rise in I_C lowers the collector voltage, which reduces the base current
questions.explanation: R_B is returned to the collector, so any increase in I_C increases the drop across R_C, lowers V_C and so reduces I_B: negative feedback.

questions.questionText: For a small-signal class A amplifier, the Q-point is usually placed near the middle of the DC load line in order to:
options: Make the transistor dissipate zero power
Allow the largest symmetrical output swing without clipping
Make β as large as possible
questions.explanation: A central Q-point leaves equal room towards saturation and cut-off, so the output can swing equally in both directions without distortion.

questions.questionText: A transistor is biased at V_CE = 5 V and I_C = 10 mA. Its quiescent collector power dissipation is:
questions.explanation: P_C = V_CE × I_C = 5 V × 10 mA = 50 mW.

questions.questionText: A BJT is in the cut-off region when:
options: Both the emitter-base and collector-base junctions are reverse biased
The emitter-base junction is forward and the collector-base junction reverse biased
The emitter-base junction is reverse and the collector-base junction forward biased
questions.explanation: In cut-off neither junction conducts, so I_C is only the tiny leakage current and the transistor acts as an open switch.

questions.questionText: An npn transistor switch (β = 100) has R_C = 1 kΩ to a 5 V supply and is driven by a 5 V logic input through R_B. With V_BE = 0.7 V and V_CE(sat) = 0.2 V, the largest R_B that still just saturates the transistor is about:
For a pnp transistor to operate in the active region:
options: The base must be more positive than the emitter, and the collector more positive than the base
The emitter and collector must both be more negative than the base
The collector must be more positive than the emitter
The emitter must be more positive than the base, and the collector more negative than the base
questions.explanation: Active operation needs the EB junction forward biased (p emitter positive with respect to the n base) and the CB junction reverse biased (p collector negative with respect to the base).

questions.questionText: The input characteristic of a transistor in the common-emitter configuration is a plot of:
options: I_C against V_CE with I_B held constant
I_C against I_B with V_CE held constant
I_B against V_BE with V_CE held constant
I_E against V_CB with I_E held constant
questions.explanation: The CE input characteristic shows base current versus base-emitter voltage at fixed V_CE; it has the shape of a forward-biased diode curve.

questions.questionText: On the common-emitter output characteristics of a BJT, each curve is drawn for a constant value of:
questions.explanation: The output family plots I_C against V_CE, with one curve for each fixed base current; in the common-base family the parameter is I_E.

questions.questionText: On a transistor's output characteristics at constant V_CE, the collector current rises from 2.0 mA to 3.0 mA when the base current rises from 20 µA to 30 µA. The AC current gain β_ac is:

In a fixed-bias circuit operating in the active region, the transistor is replaced by one whose β is twice as large, with all resistors and V_CC unchanged. Provided it stays in the active region, the collector current:
questions.explanation: In fixed bias I_B = (V_CC − V_BE)/R_B does not depend on β, so I_C = βI_B doubles; this sensitivity is the main weakness of fixed bias.

questions.questionText: A BJT is called a bipolar device because:
options: It can be operated from positive and negative supplies
Both electrons and holes take part in conduction
questions.explanation: Current in a BJT involves both majority and minority carriers, that is both electrons and holes, unlike the unipolar FET.

questions.questionText: Punch-through (reach-through) in a BJT occurs when:
options: The collector depletion region spreads across the whole base and meets the emitter depletion region
The base current exceeds the collector current
The emitter-base junction is forward biased by more than 0.7 V
questions.explanation: At very high collector voltage the depletion layer widens through the thin base until it reaches the emitter junction, and a large current flows that is no longer controlled by the base.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the BJT is NOT correct?
options: The base is thin and lightly doped
The collector current in the active region is controlled mainly by the base-emitter junction
The emitter and collector can be interchanged without any change in performance
β varies with temperature and collector current
questions.explanation: The emitter and collector differ in doping and size, so reversing them gives a much smaller current gain; the other statements are correct.

subtopics.title: MOSFET (Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor FET)
subtopics.subtitle: Insulated gate, threshold voltage, square-law operation and MOSFET vs JFET vs BJT

concepts.text: Field Effect Transistors

FETs (JFET, MOSFET) are voltage-controlled: the gate-source voltage controls the drain current, drawing virtually no gate current. MOSFETs dominate modern digital electronics. In a JFET the gate is a reverse-biased pn junction; in a MOSFET the gate is completely insulated from the channel by a thin layer of silicon dioxide, which is why it is also called an insulated-gate FET (IGFET). FETs are unipolar devices: current is carried by one type of carrier only, electrons in an n-channel device and holes in a p-channel device.
MOSFET Structure

An n-channel MOSFET is built on a p-type substrate, the body. Two heavily doped n+ regions form the source and drain, and between them the gate, a metal or polysilicon electrode, sits on a SiO₂ layer only a few nanometres thick. The four terminals are gate (G), source (S), drain (D) and body (B); in discrete devices the body is tied internally to the source, which also creates a body diode between drain and source. A p-channel MOSFET is the complement: p+ source and drain in an n-type substrate, operated with negative gate and drain voltages relative to the source.
Enhancement and Depletion Types
The two MOSFET families and how they differ at V_GS = 0:
items: Enhancement mode (normally OFF): no channel exists at V_GS = 0. A gate voltage above the threshold V_T attracts electrons under the oxide and creates (enhances) an inversion channel. The symbol shows a broken channel line, with the body arrow pointing inward for n-channel and outward for p-channel.

Depletion mode (normally ON): a channel is built in during manufacture, so drain current flows at V_GS = 0. A negative V_GS (n-channel) depletes the channel and reduces the current; a positive V_GS enhances it. The symbol shows a solid, continuous channel line.
Enhancement n-channel devices are by far the most common in digital ICs and power switching, because a normally-off switch is safer and easier to drive.

concepts.text: Threshold Voltage, Regions and Characteristics

The threshold voltage V_T (also written V_th or V_GS(th)) is the minimum gate-source voltage needed to form the channel, typically 0.5 to 2 V in small-signal ICs and 2 to 4 V in power devices. The excess V_GS − V_T is called the overdrive voltage. Which region the device is in depends on how V_DS compares with this overdrive.

rows: V_GS > V_T and V_DS < V_GS − V_T
Rises with V_DS, roughly linear at small V_DS
V_GS > V_T and V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T
I_D = k(V_GS − V_T)², independent of V_DS

concepts.plainText: ID = k (VGS - VT)^2   with k = (1/2) mu_n Cox (W/L)   (saturation)
ID = k [2 (VGS - VT) VDS - VDS^2]   (ohmic region)

concepts.text: The drain (output) characteristic plots I_D against V_DS for several values of V_GS: each curve rises steeply in the ohmic region and then flattens into saturation, with a higher curve for each higher V_GS. The transfer characteristic plots I_D against V_GS at constant V_DS: it is zero below V_T and then rises as a parabola. Its slope is the transconductance g_m = 2k(V_GS − V_T) = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_T), the gain parameter of a MOSFET amplifier. The very high input impedance (10^12 Ω or more) means the gate draws essentially only leakage current, so the DC input power is negligible.
Handling, Comparison and Uses

The gate oxide is so thin that a static discharge of a few tens of volts can puncture it permanently. MOSFETs are therefore shipped with the leads shorted or in conductive foam, handled at grounded workstations, and many ICs include protective diodes on every input. A gate must never be left floating in a circuit, because any stray charge can turn the device partly on.

rows: Low noise, stable (I_D falls as temperature rises)

concepts.text: Applications:
items: Switching: a near-ideal switch with very low on-resistance and negligible gate drive power in the steady state.
Digital ICs: CMOS logic, microprocessors, SRAM and flash memory (a floating-gate MOSFET stores each bit).
Power electronics: switch-mode power supplies, motor drives and inverters switching at tens to hundreds of kHz.
Analog circuits: high-input-impedance amplifiers, current mirrors and analog switches.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: MOSFET Analysis and Biasing

The square law comes from the charge in the channel. Once V_GS exceeds V_T, the inversion charge per unit area at a point x along the channel is C_ox(V_GS − V_T − v(x)), where v(x) is the local channel voltage that rises from 0 at the source to V_DS at the drain. The drift current is this charge times the electron velocity μ_n E, and integrating from source to drain gives the ohmic-region equation. When V_DS reaches V_GS − V_T the charge at the drain end falls to zero (pinch-off); beyond that point the extra voltage drops across the short pinched region and the current stays at its peak value, which is the saturation equation.

concepts.plainText: ID = mu_n Cox (W/L) [ (VGS - VT) VDS - VDS^2 / 2 ]   (same as k[2 Vov VDS - VDS^2] with k = mu_n Cox W / 2L)

concepts.text: Two second-order effects matter in practice. Channel-length modulation: in saturation the pinch-off point moves slightly towards the source as V_DS rises, so the effective channel shortens and I_D creeps up with V_DS; this is modelled by the factor (1 + λV_DS) and gives the finite output resistance r_o = 1/(λI_D). Body effect: if the source is above the body potential, the extra reverse bias widens the depletion layer under the gate and raises V_T, which is why stacked transistors in an IC have slightly higher thresholds.

concepts.plainText: ID = k (VGS - VT)^2 (1 + lambda VDS);   ro = 1 / (lambda ID)

concepts.text: JFETs and depletion MOSFETs obey the Shockley equation instead of the enhancement square law. Here I_DSS is the drain current at V_GS = 0 and V_P (the pinch-off voltage, negative for n-channel) is the gate voltage at which the channel is fully depleted. A depletion MOSFET can also be driven with positive V_GS, where the same equation predicts I_D above I_DSS; a JFET cannot, because its gate junction would become forward biased.

concepts.plainText: ID = IDSS (1 - VGS/VP)^2;   gm = (2 IDSS / |VP|)(1 - VGS/VP)

rows: V_GS = V_G from a divider, source grounded
R_G from drain to gate, so V_GS = V_DS
V_GS = V_DD − I_D R_D, device always saturated

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: divider plus source resistor (E-MOSFET)
Given: V_G = 6 V, R_S = 1 kΩ, V_T = 2 V, k = 1 mA/V²
Loop:   V_GS = V_G − I_D R_S = 6 − I_D   (I_D in mA)
Device: I_D = (V_GS − 2)²
Let x = V_GS − 2:  2 + x = 6 − x²  ->  x² + x − 4 = 0
x = (−1 + √17)/2 = 1.56 V   (other root −2.56 V gives V_GS < V_T, reject)
I_D = x² = 2.44 mA,  V_GS = 3.56 V
Check: V_DS must be at least V_GS − V_T = 1.56 V for saturation

Worked example 2: common-source gain with r_o
Given: I_D = 1 mA, V_GS − V_T = 1 V, λ = 0.02 V⁻¹, R_D = 10 kΩ
g_m = 2 I_D/(V_GS − V_T) = 2 × 1/1 = 2 mA/V
r_o = 1/(λ I_D) = 1/(0.02 × 1 mA) = 50 kΩ
R_D ∥ r_o = (10 × 50)/(10 + 50) = 8.33 kΩ
A_v = −g_m (R_D ∥ r_o) = −2 × 8.33 = −16.7
Ignoring r_o would give −20, a 20 % overestimate
Common mistakes in MOSFET problems:
items: Squaring a negative overdrive: if V_GS < V_T the device is off and I_D = 0, not k(V_GS − V_T)².
Using the saturation equation without checking V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T; if the check fails, redo the problem with the ohmic equation.
Keeping the wrong root of the bias quadratic: reject any root that makes V_GS < V_T (enhancement) or V_GS beyond V_P (JFET or depletion).
Mixing k conventions: some books write I_D = (k'/2)(W/L)(V_GS − V_T)², so k in the form used here already contains the factor one half.
Forgetting that for a p-channel device V_GS, V_DS and V_T are all negative; work with magnitudes and then give the current direction (source to drain).

concepts.text: Every biasing problem follows the same three steps: write the loop equation for V_GS, substitute the device equation, then solve and check the region. Two roots always appear in a quadratic bias problem and exactly one of them is physical.

formulas.plainText: ID = k (VGS - VT)^2   in saturation, VDS >= VGS - VT
ID = k [2 (VGS - VT) VDS - VDS^2]   in the ohmic region

notes.text: BJT is current-controlled; FET is voltage-controlled. Examiners regularly test exactly this contrast.

Enhancement = normally OFF, channel created by V_GS (broken line in the symbol). Depletion = normally ON, channel depleted by V_GS (solid line). Questions often simply ask which type conducts at V_GS = 0.

The saturation region of a MOSFET is its amplifying (constant-current) region, the opposite of the BJT, where saturation means fully ON. In MOSFET language the fully-on switch state is the ohmic (triode) region.
Doubling the overdrive V_GS − V_T quadruples I_D in saturation because of the square law. Always check the region first: if V_DS < V_GS − V_T, use the ohmic equation instead.

formulas.title: MOSFET Saturation Current (Square Law)
formulas.description: Drain current when VGS > VT and VDS >= VGS - VT; k is the device constant in A/V² and VT the threshold voltage.

formulas.title: MOSFET Device Constant
formulas.description: mu_n is the channel mobility, Cox the gate-oxide capacitance per unit area and W/L the channel width-to-length ratio; some texts write the same constant as K/2 or kn'(W/L)/2.

formulas.title: MOSFET Ohmic-Region Current
formulas.description: Valid for VGS > VT and VDS < VGS - VT; for very small VDS the device behaves as a resistor.

formulas.title: MOSFET Transconductance
formulas.description: Small-signal gain parameter in saturation, the slope of the transfer characteristic; the voltage gain of a common-source stage is about -gm RD.

formulas.title: MOSFET On-Resistance
formulas.description: Channel resistance deep in the ohmic region (small VDS); a larger gate overdrive gives a lower on-resistance switch.

flashcards.front: What is the threshold voltage of a MOSFET?
flashcards.back: The minimum V_GS needed to form a conducting channel in an enhancement MOSFET; below it the device is cut off. Typically 0.5 to 2 V in ICs, 2 to 4 V in power devices.

flashcards.front: Why does a MOSFET have such a high input impedance?
flashcards.back: The gate is insulated from the channel by SiO₂, so no DC gate current flows other than leakage; the input impedance is 10^12 Ω or more.

flashcards.front: How does MOSFET saturation differ from BJT saturation?
flashcards.back: MOSFET saturation is the constant-current amplifying region (V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T); BJT saturation is the fully-on switch state with both junctions forward biased.

flashcards.front: Why must MOSFETs be protected against static electricity?
flashcards.back: The gate oxide is only a few nanometres thick and breaks down at a few tens of volts, so an electrostatic discharge can puncture it permanently.

questions.questionText: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET has V_T = 2 V and k = 0.5 mA/V². When it operates in saturation with V_GS = 4 V, the drain current is:
Which type of MOSFET carries drain current when the gate-source voltage is zero?
questions.explanation: A depletion-mode MOSFET has a channel built in during manufacture and is normally ON; V_GS is used to deplete it. Enhancement devices have no channel until V_GS exceeds the threshold.

questions.questionText: An n-channel MOSFET has V_GS = 5 V and V_T = 1 V. It operates in the saturation region when V_DS is:
questions.explanation: Saturation requires V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T = 5 − 1 = 4 V. For V_DS below 4 V the device is in the ohmic (triode) region.

questions.questionText: When an n-channel enhancement MOSFET is biased with V_GS above its threshold voltage, the conducting channel between source and drain is:
options: A layer of holes attracted to the surface of an n-type substrate
An inversion layer of electrons induced at the surface of the p-type substrate under the gate
An n-type region diffused between source and drain during manufacture
The depletion region around the reverse-biased drain junction
questions.explanation: A positive gate repels holes and attracts electrons to the surface of the p-type body; above V_T the surface inverts to n-type and links the n+ source and drain. A channel diffused in during manufacture is the feature of a depletion-mode device.

questions.questionText: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET has V_T = 2 V and k = 1 mA/V². With V_GS = 1.5 V and V_DS = 10 V, the drain current is:
options: 0 mA, because the device is in cut-off
questions.explanation: V_GS = 1.5 V is below V_T = 2 V, so no channel forms and I_D ≈ 0. Squaring (V_GS − V_T) = −0.5 V to get 0.25 mA is a classic error: the square law applies only when V_GS > V_T.

questions.questionText: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET has k = 0.4 mA/V² and V_T = 1 V. In saturation with V_GS = 3.5 V, the drain current is:
An n-channel enhancement MOSFET with k = 0.5 mA/V² and V_T = 1 V is biased in saturation at V_GS = 3 V. Its transconductance g_m is:
An n-channel enhancement MOSFET has k = 0.5 mA/V² and V_T = 1 V. With V_GS = 4 V and V_DS = 1 V, the drain current is:
questions.explanation: V_DS = 1 V is less than V_GS − V_T = 3 V, so the device is in the ohmic region: I_D = k[2(V_GS − V_T)V_DS − V_DS²] = 0.5 × (2 × 3 × 1 − 1²) = 2.5 mA. The saturation formula would wrongly give 4.5 mA.

questions.questionText: In a common-source stage, V_DD = 12 V, R_D = 2 kΩ and the gate bias sets V_GS = 4 V. The n-channel enhancement MOSFET has V_T = 2 V and k = 0.5 mA/V². The drain-source voltage V_DS is:
questions.explanation: I_D = 0.5 × (4 − 2)² = 2 mA, so V_DS = 12 − 2 mA × 2 kΩ = 8 V. Since 8 V ≥ V_GS − V_T = 2 V, the saturation assumption holds.

questions.questionText: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET (V_T = 2 V, k = 0.25 mA/V²) has its gate fed from a divider R1 = 1 MΩ (to V_DD) and R2 = 500 kΩ (to ground), with V_DD = 15 V, R_D = 3 kΩ and the source grounded. V_DS is:
questions.explanation: V_G = 15 × 0.5/1.5 = 5 V = V_GS (no gate current). I_D = 0.25 × (5 − 2)² = 2.25 mA, so V_DS = 15 − 2.25 × 3 = 8.25 V, which exceeds V_GS − V_T = 3 V, confirming saturation.

questions.questionText: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET with V_T = 2 V and k = 1 mA/V² has V_G = 6 V set by a divider and a source resistor R_S = 1 kΩ. Assuming saturation, the drain current is approximately:
questions.explanation: V_GS = 6 − I_D × 1 kΩ and I_D = (V_GS − 2)². With x = V_GS − 2: x² + x − 4 = 0, so x = 1.56 V and I_D = x² ≈ 2.44 mA. The other root (6.56 mA) makes V_GS negative, below V_T, and is rejected.

questions.questionText: A MOSFET in saturation carries I_D = 2 mA with an overdrive V_GS − V_T = 0.5 V. Its transconductance is:
questions.explanation: g_m = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_T) = 2 × 2 mA/0.5 V = 8 mA/V.

questions.questionText: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET with k = 1 mA/V² is biased in saturation at I_D = 4 mA. Its transconductance is:
questions.explanation: From I_D = k(V_GS − V_T)², the overdrive is √(4/1) = 2 V, so g_m = 2k(V_GS − V_T) = 2√(kI_D) = 2 × 1 × 2 = 4 mA/V.

questions.questionText: A common-source MOSFET amplifier with a bypassed source has g_m = 3 mA/V and R_D = 4 kΩ (r_o neglected). Its small-signal voltage gain is:
questions.explanation: A_v = −g_m R_D = −3 mA/V × 4 kΩ = −12. The minus sign shows the 180° phase inversion of the common-source stage.

questions.questionText: A common-source stage has I_D = 1 mA, g_m = 2 mA/V, channel-length modulation λ = 0.02 V⁻¹ and R_D = 10 kΩ. Including r_o, the voltage gain is approximately:
A MOSFET with channel-length modulation parameter λ = 0.01 V⁻¹ is biased at I_D = 2 mA. Its output resistance r_o is:
An n-channel enhancement MOSFET with V_T = 1 V carries 2 mA in saturation at V_GS = 3 V. If V_GS is raised to 5 V (still in saturation), the drain current becomes:
questions.explanation: I_D is proportional to (V_GS − V_T)²: the overdrive doubles from 2 V to 4 V, so I_D = 2 × (4/2)² = 8 mA. Forgetting V_T gives 2 × (5/3)² = 5.56 mA.

questions.questionText: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET has k = 0.5 mA/V² and V_T = 1.5 V. The gate-source voltage needed for I_D = 2 mA in saturation is:
A MOSFET has μ_nC_ox = 200 µA/V², W/L = 10 and V_T = 0.5 V, with k = ½μ_nC_ox(W/L). In saturation at V_GS = 1.5 V, the drain current is:
questions.explanation: k = ½ × 200 µA/V² × 10 = 1 mA/V², and I_D = k(V_GS − V_T)² = 1 × (1.5 − 0.5)² = 1 mA. Dropping the ½ gives 2 mA; forgetting W/L gives 0.1 mA.

questions.questionText: A MOSFET switch with k = 2 mA/V² and V_T = 2 V is driven at V_GS = 7 V and carries a small V_DS. Its on-resistance r_DS(on) is approximately:
questions.explanation: For small V_DS, r_DS(on) ≈ 1/[2k(V_GS − V_T)] = 1/(2 × 2 × 10⁻³ × 5) = 50 Ω.

questions.questionText: A power MOSFET with R_DS(on) = 0.05 Ω switches a 10 A load current with a 50 % duty cycle. Neglecting switching losses, its average conduction loss is:
A p-channel enhancement MOSFET has V_T = −2 V and k = 0.2 mA/V². In saturation with V_GS = −5 V, the magnitude of the drain current is:
questions.explanation: I_D = k(V_GS − V_T)² = 0.2 × (−5 + 2)² = 0.2 × 9 = 1.8 mA, flowing from source to drain. Adding the magnitudes, (5 + 2)², gives the wrong 9.8 mA.

questions.questionText: A p-channel enhancement MOSFET with V_T = −1.5 V conducts when:
options: V_GS is more negative than −1.5 V
V_GS is more positive than +1.5 V
V_GS is between −1.5 V and 0 V
questions.explanation: A p-channel enhancement device needs the gate driven negative with respect to the source, beyond the (negative) threshold, to attract holes and form the channel.

questions.questionText: An n-channel depletion MOSFET has I_DSS = 8 mA and V_P = −4 V. At V_GS = −2 V, the drain current is:
An n-channel depletion MOSFET with I_DSS = 8 mA and V_P = −4 V is operated at V_GS = +1 V. The drain current is:
questions.explanation: A positive gate enhances the built-in channel: I_D = 8 × (1 − 1/(−4))² = 8 × 1.25² = 12.5 mA, above I_DSS.

questions.questionText: Which device can be operated in both depletion and enhancement modes, that is, with its drain current controlled by either polarity of V_GS while the gate current stays negligible?
questions.explanation: The insulated gate of a D-MOSFET allows positive or negative V_GS. A JFET gate junction becomes forward biased if driven the wrong way, and an E-MOSFET simply stays off for one polarity.

questions.questionText: An n-channel JFET has I_DSS = 10 mA and V_P = −5 V. Its transconductance at V_GS = −2 V is:
An n-channel depletion MOSFET (I_DSS = 6 mA, V_P = −3 V) is self-biased: the gate is returned to ground through R_G and R_S = 1 kΩ is in the source. The drain current is:
questions.explanation: V_GS = −I_D R_S, so I_D = 6(1 − I_D/3)², giving I_D² − 7.5I_D + 9 = 0 with roots 1.5 mA and 6 mA. The 6 mA root makes V_GS = −6 V, beyond V_P, so I_D = 1.5 mA (V_GS = −1.5 V).

questions.questionText: The input resistance of a MOSFET is much higher than that of a JFET because:
options: The MOSFET gate is insulated from the channel by silicon dioxide, while the JFET gate is a reverse-biased pn junction
The MOSFET channel is much longer than a JFET channel
The MOSFET is a bipolar device
The JFET gate junction is forward biased in normal operation
questions.explanation: A reverse-biased junction still passes a small leakage current (input resistance about 10^8 Ω), whereas the oxide insulator passes practically none (10^12 Ω or more).

questions.questionText: In an n-channel enhancement MOSFET, the substrate (body) is made of:
questions.explanation: The n+ source and drain sit in a p-type body; the n-type channel is formed by inverting the surface of this p-type material.

questions.questionText: In its saturation region, a MOSFET behaves mainly as:
options: A closed switch with very low resistance
A current source whose value is set by V_GS
A resistor whose value is set by V_GS
questions.explanation: In saturation I_D = k(V_GS − V_T)² is nearly independent of V_DS, so the device acts as a voltage-controlled current source, which is why amplifiers are biased there.

questions.questionText: Which statement about an n-channel enhancement MOSFET is NOT correct?
options: In saturation the drain current rises in proportion to V_DS
The steady-state gate current is practically zero
No drain current flows until V_GS exceeds V_T
Its circuit symbol shows a broken line for the channel
questions.explanation: In saturation I_D is almost independent of V_DS (only a slight rise from channel-length modulation). The other three statements are true.

questions.questionText: When V_DS of a MOSFET is increased to V_GS − V_T, the channel:
options: Pinches off at the drain end, and further increases in V_DS barely change I_D
Disappears completely, so I_D falls to zero
Pinches off at the source end and the current reverses
Widens uniformly, so I_D starts rising faster
questions.explanation: At V_DS = V_GS − V_T the gate-to-channel voltage at the drain end drops to V_T and the inversion charge there falls to zero. Current still flows through the pinched region, but it saturates.

questions.questionText: Power MOSFETs can be connected in parallel to share a large current without special balancing, mainly because:
options: Their threshold voltages are exactly equal from device to device
Their drain current rises with temperature
Their on-resistance rises with temperature, so a hotter device takes less current
questions.explanation: Carrier mobility falls as temperature rises, so R_DS(on) has a positive temperature coefficient; a device that heats up conducts less, which balances the current. A BJT behaves the opposite way and can suffer thermal runaway.

questions.questionText: If the source of an n-channel MOSFET is at a higher potential than its p-type body, the threshold voltage:
options: Becomes negative, so the device is always on
questions.explanation: The extra source-to-body reverse bias widens the depletion region under the gate, so more gate voltage is needed to create inversion: V_T increases.

questions.questionText: MOSFETs are stored in conductive foam or with their leads shorted together because:
options: The drain junction is damaged by light
Static charge can puncture the very thin gate oxide
The body diode is damaged by moisture
The channel slowly loses its doping in storage
questions.explanation: The gate oxide is only nanometres thick and has very high resistance, so static charge builds up a voltage that can break it down permanently.

questions.questionText: The transfer characteristic (I_D versus V_GS in saturation) of an n-channel enhancement MOSFET is:
options: A straight line through the origin
Maximum at V_GS = 0 and falling to zero at V_P
Zero up to V_T and then a rising parabola
An exponential curve like that of a diode
questions.explanation: I_D = k(V_GS − V_T)² for V_GS > V_T and zero below it. A curve that is maximum at V_GS = 0 describes a JFET or depletion MOSFET.

questions.questionText: For very small V_DS (well below V_GS − V_T), a MOSFET behaves as:
options: A resistor whose value is controlled by V_GS
questions.explanation: With V_DS small, the ohmic equation reduces to I_D ≈ 2k(V_GS − V_T)V_DS, a straight line through the origin whose slope is set by V_GS: a voltage-controlled resistor.

questions.questionText: For the same dimensions and overdrive, an n-channel MOSFET carries more current than a p-channel MOSFET because:
options: Electron mobility is about two to three times hole mobility
The n-channel device has a thicker gate oxide
Holes carry a larger charge than electrons
The p-channel threshold voltage is always zero
questions.explanation: k is proportional to carrier mobility, and in silicon μ_n is roughly 2 to 3 times μ_p, so pMOS devices must be made wider to match nMOS drive.

questions.questionText: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET (k = 1 mA/V², V_T = 1 V) has V_GS = 3 V, R_D = 4 kΩ and V_DD = 10 V. The drain-source voltage is approximately:
questions.explanation: Assuming saturation gives I_D = 4 mA and V_DS = 10 − 16 = −6 V, which is impossible, so the device is ohmic. Solving I_D = 4V_DS − V_DS² with V_DS = 10 − 4I_D gives 4V_DS² − 17V_DS + 10 = 0, so V_DS ≈ 0.71 V (the 3.55 V root exceeds V_GS − V_T = 2 V and is rejected).

questions.questionText: In the circuit symbol of an enhancement MOSFET, an arrow on the body lead pointing inward towards the channel indicates:
questions.explanation: The arrow shows the p-body to n-channel junction direction (p to n, like a diode arrow), so inward means n-channel; outward means p-channel.

questions.questionText: A MOSFET has its gate connected to its drain (k = 0.5 mA/V², V_T = 1 V) and carries I_D = 2 mA. Its V_GS is:
questions.explanation: With gate tied to drain, V_DS = V_GS > V_GS − V_T, so the device is always saturated: V_GS = V_T + √(I_D/k) = 1 + √4 = 3 V.

questions.questionText: A MOSFET source follower has g_m = 4 mA/V and R_S = 1 kΩ (r_o neglected). Its voltage gain is:
questions.explanation: A_v = g_m R_S/(1 + g_m R_S) = 4/(1 + 4) = 0.8, positive and a little below one.

questions.questionText: In a discrete n-channel power MOSFET with the body tied to the source, the intrinsic body diode:
options: Conducts from drain to source whenever V_GS exceeds V_T
Conducts from source to drain when the drain is driven below the source
Is connected between gate and source to protect the oxide
questions.explanation: The p-type body (anode, tied to the source) and the n-type drain (cathode) form a diode, so it conducts when the drain goes negative with respect to the source, for example with an inductive load.

questions.questionText: Compared with a BJT, a main advantage of a MOSFET used as a switch is:
options: Current is carried by both electrons and holes
It is controlled by input current rather than voltage
Negligible steady-state drive current because the gate is insulated
Its gate forms a forward-biased pn junction with the channel
questions.explanation: The MOSFET is a voltage-controlled, unipolar device with an insulated gate, so once the gate capacitance is charged no drive current is needed to hold it on.

questions.questionText: A power MOSFET needs a total gate charge Q_g = 20 nC to switch on and is switched at 100 kHz. The average gate-drive current is:
questions.explanation: I_avg = Q_g × f = 20 × 10⁻⁹ × 100 × 10³ = 2 × 10⁻³ A = 2 mA. Although the DC gate current is zero, charging the gate capacitance every cycle needs real drive current.

questions.questionText: An n-channel depletion MOSFET (I_DSS = 10 mA, V_P = −5 V) is fixed-biased at V_GS = −2 V with V_DD = 20 V and R_D = 2 kΩ. V_DS is:
questions.explanation: I_D = 10 × (1 − (−2)/(−5))² = 10 × 0.6² = 3.6 mA, so V_DS = 20 − 3.6 × 2 = 12.8 V, well above V_GS − V_P = 3 V, so the device is saturated.

questions.questionText: Self-bias (gate returned to ground through R_G, resistor R_S in the source) is used with JFETs and depletion MOSFETs but not with an n-channel enhancement MOSFET because:
options: It can only make V_GS zero or negative, which keeps an enhancement device below threshold and off
The gate current through R_G would be too large
It makes V_GS too positive for an enhancement device
Enhancement MOSFETs have no separate source terminal
questions.explanation: With the gate at 0 V and the source at +I_D R_S, V_GS = −I_D R_S ≤ 0. An n-channel E-MOSFET needs V_GS above a positive V_T, so it needs a divider or drain-feedback bias.

questions.questionText: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET (k = 0.5 mA/V², V_T = 2 V) uses drain-feedback bias: a large R_G connects drain to gate, with R_D = 2 kΩ and V_DD = 12 V. The drain current is approximately:
questions.explanation: No gate current flows, so V_GS = V_DS = 12 − 2I_D and I_D = 0.5(V_GS − 2)². With x = V_GS − 2: x² + x − 10 = 0, x = 2.70 V, so I_D = 0.5 × 2.70² ≈ 3.65 mA (V_GS ≈ 4.70 V). The other root gives V_GS below V_T and is rejected.

subtopics.title: CMOS (Complementary MOS)
subtopics.subtitle: nMOS-pMOS pairs, the CMOS inverter, power dissipation, noise margins and CMOS vs TTL

concepts.text: Complementary MOS

CMOS technology builds every logic gate from complementary enhancement MOSFETs: n-channel devices in a pull-down network connected to ground and p-channel devices in a pull-up network connected to V_DD. The two networks are logical duals, so for any valid input combination exactly one of them conducts. Because it uses both n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs, CMOS combines very low power consumption with high noise immunity, and it is the dominant technology for microprocessors, memories and digital ICs.
The CMOS Inverter

The inverter has one nMOS (source to ground) and one pMOS (source to V_DD) with their gates joined as the input and their drains joined as the output. With the input LOW (0 V) the nMOS is off and the pMOS is on, so the output is pulled up to V_DD. With the input HIGH (V_DD) the nMOS is on and the pMOS is off, so the output is pulled down to 0 V. In either steady state one transistor is off, so no DC path exists between V_DD and ground and the output swings the full rail-to-rail range.

rows: In transition; brief supply current spike

concepts.text: Power Dissipation

Static power is almost zero because in steady state only sub-threshold and junction leakage flows, of the order of nanowatts per gate. Power is consumed while switching: charging the load capacitance C to V_DD and discharging it to ground dissipates C·V_DD² per cycle, so the dynamic power is P = C·V_DD²·f. A short-circuit component is added during the moment both transistors conduct. Dynamic power therefore grows with clock frequency and with the square of the supply voltage, which is why supply voltages have fallen from 5 V to about 1 V in modern processors.

concepts.plainText: P_dyn = C x VDD^2 x f

concepts.text: Noise Margins, Fan-out and Speed
What makes CMOS robust and fast, and its one weakness:
items: Noise margins: the inverter switches sharply near V_DD/2 and the logic levels sit close to the rails, so NM_H = V_OH − V_IH and NM_L = V_IL − V_OL are each roughly 30 % of V_DD, about 1.5 V at a 5 V supply against 0.4 V for TTL. This is the source of the high noise immunity of CMOS.
Input impedance and fan-out: every input is an insulated gate, so one output can drive 50 or more inputs; the limit is the added capacitance, which slows the edges, not DC loading.
Speed-power trade-off: propagation delay is roughly proportional to C·V_DD/I_D, so raising V_DD speeds the gate up but increases power as V_DD². The power-delay product is the usual figure of merit.

Latch-up: parasitic pnp and npn transistors in the substrate can form a thyristor-like path from V_DD to ground if an input or output is driven beyond the supply rails. Guard rings and clamp diodes prevent it, and unused inputs must never be left floating.

concepts.text: CMOS versus TTL

rows: About 10 nW static, rises with frequency
About 8 to 10 ns (74HC); 4000 series much slower
High (margins about 30 % of V_DD, about 1.5 V at 5 V)

concepts.text: Logic Families and Applications
CMOS logic families and where CMOS is used:
items: 4000 series: the original CMOS family with a 3 to 15 V supply; very low power but slow (tens of nanoseconds) and with weak output drive.
74HC and 74HCT: high-speed CMOS with TTL-comparable speed; 74HCT has TTL-compatible input levels for mixed systems. 74AC, 74LVC and lower-voltage families followed.
Memory: an SRAM cell is a six-transistor CMOS latch, DRAM uses one MOSFET and one capacitor per bit, and flash uses floating-gate MOSFETs.
Microprocessors, microcontrollers, FPGAs and image sensors are all fabricated in CMOS, because only its near-zero static power allows billions of transistors on one chip.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: CMOS Inverter and Gate Design

The voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) of the inverter can be traced by sweeping the input from 0 to V_DD and noting the region of each transistor. The output stays at V_DD until the nMOS turns on, falls steeply through the middle where both transistors are saturated and the gain is highest, and settles at 0 V once the pMOS turns off. The steepness of this middle section is what places V_IL and V_IH close to each other and gives CMOS its wide noise margins.

The switching threshold V_M is the input voltage at which V_out = V_in. Equating the two saturation currents, k_n(V_M − V_tn)² = k_p(V_DD − V_M − |V_tp|)², gives the formula below. With matched devices (k_n = k_p, V_tn = |V_tp|) V_M = V_DD/2; a stronger nMOS pulls V_M lower and a stronger pMOS pushes it higher. Because μ_n is about 2 to 3 times μ_p, the pMOS is normally made that much wider to centre V_M.

concepts.plainText: VM = (Vtn + r (VDD - |Vtp|)) / (1 + r),  r = sqrt(kp / kn)

concepts.text: The C·V²·f law follows from energy accounting. Charging the load from 0 to V_DD draws charge Q = C·V_DD from the supply, so the supply delivers Q·V_DD = C·V_DD² of energy. Half of it, ½C·V_DD², ends up stored on the capacitor and the other half is lost as heat in the pMOS; on the falling edge the stored half is dissipated in the nMOS. One complete charge-discharge cycle therefore dissipates C·V_DD², independent of the transistor resistances. In a real chip only a fraction α of the nodes switch each clock cycle, and leakage adds a static term.

Worked example 1: power of a processor core
Given: 10^6 gates, C = 10 fF each, α = 0.1, V_DD = 1.2 V, f = 1 GHz, I_leak = 100 mA
P_dyn  = α N C V_DD² f
       = 0.1 × 10^6 × 10×10^-15 × 1.44 × 10^9 = 1.44 W
P_stat = V_DD × I_leak = 1.2 × 0.1 = 0.12 W
P_total = 1.44 + 0.12 = 1.56 W
Dropping V_DD to 1.0 V: P_dyn = 1.44 × (1.0/1.2)² = 1.0 W

A static CMOS gate always has an nMOS pull-down network and a dual pMOS pull-up network with one transistor pair per input. Series nMOS implement AND inside the inversion, parallel nMOS implement OR, and the pull-up network swaps every series connection for a parallel one and vice versa. Transistors in series add their on-resistances, so series stacks must be widened: each of n series devices needs about n times the width of a single device for the same drive. This is why NAND (series nMOS, fast electrons) is preferred to NOR (series pMOS, slow holes).

Worked example 2: worst-case delay of a 2-input NOR
Given: each pMOS R_on = 2 kΩ, each nMOS R_on = 1 kΩ, C_L = 50 fF
Pull-up: two pMOS in series -> R = 4 kΩ
t_pLH = 0.69 × 4×10^3 × 50×10^-15 = 138 ps

Average t_p = (138 + 34.5)/2 = 86 ps
Common mistakes with CMOS questions:
items: Treating static power as the main loss: in active logic dynamic power C·V²·f dominates, while leakage matters mostly in idle or very dense chips.
Forgetting that power scales with V_DD squared: halving V_DD alone cuts dynamic power to one quarter, not one half.
Swapping the NAND and NOR structures: NAND = series nMOS and parallel pMOS; NOR = parallel nMOS and series pMOS.
Mixing up the noise-margin formulas: NM_H = V_OH − V_IH and NM_L = V_IL − V_OL, always output level minus input threshold on the same side.
Assuming CMOS fan-out is limited by DC current: it is limited by load capacitance and the resulting slower edges.

concepts.text: A standard TTL output guarantees only V_OH = 2.7 V, below the 3.15 V V_IH of a 74HC input at 4.5 V, so the HIGH noise margin is negative. Use a 74HCT part (TTL-compatible input thresholds) or a pull-up resistor when TTL drives CMOS.

formulas.plainText: P_total = VDD I_leak + alpha C VDD^2 f   (alpha = activity factor)

formulas.latex: NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH}, \qquad NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL}
formulas.plainText: NM_H = VOH - VIH;   NM_L = VIL - VOL

notes.text: CMOS = both nMOS and pMOS in every gate. Its two headline advantages are very low power and high noise immunity; static power is nearly zero and dynamic power is P = C·V²·f.
Never leave a CMOS input floating: it can drift to mid-supply, turn both transistors partly on and waste power, oscillate or trigger latch-up. Tie unused inputs to V_DD or ground.
Halving V_DD cuts dynamic power to one quarter, which is why IC supply voltages have fallen steadily, but it also slows the gate because the overdrive V_GS − V_T shrinks.
In the CMOS inverter the pMOS is the pull-up and the nMOS is the pull-down. In steady state exactly one of them is on; both conduct only momentarily during a transition.

formulas.description: Switching power of a CMOS node with load capacitance C, supply VDD and switching frequency f; linear in f, quadratic in VDD.

formulas.title: Total CMOS Power

formulas.description: Static (leakage) term plus dynamic term; alpha is the activity factor, the fraction of clock cycles in which the node switches.
