flashcards.front: In a CMOS inverter, which transistor is on when the input is HIGH?
flashcards.back: The nMOS (pull-down) is on and the pMOS (pull-up) is off, so the output is pulled LOW to 0 V.

flashcards.front: Why is the static power of CMOS nearly zero?
flashcards.back: In either logic state one of the two series transistors is off, so there is no DC path from V_DD to ground; only leakage current flows.

flashcards.front: How does CMOS dynamic power depend on supply voltage and frequency?
flashcards.back: P = C·V_DD²·f: linear in frequency and load capacitance, quadratic in supply voltage.

flashcards.front: What is latch-up in CMOS?
flashcards.back: A parasitic thyristor formed by substrate pnp and npn transistors that turns on when a pin is driven beyond the supply rails, creating a low-impedance path from V_DD to ground.

questions.questionText: A CMOS gate drives a 10 pF load from a 5 V supply and switches at 10 MHz. Its dynamic power dissipation is approximately:
When the input of a CMOS inverter is LOW, which statement is correct?
options: Both transistors are on and the output sits at V_DD/2
The nMOS is on and the output is LOW
Both transistors are off and the output floats
The pMOS is on, the nMOS is off and the output is HIGH
questions.explanation: A LOW input gives V_GS = 0 for the nMOS (off) and V_GS = −V_DD for the pMOS (on), so the pull-up transistor connects the output to V_DD.

questions.questionText: A CMOS bus driver switches a 20 pF load at 50 MHz from a 3.3 V supply. Its dynamic power is approximately:
A CMOS circuit dissipates 40 mW of dynamic power at V_DD = 5 V. If V_DD is reduced to 2.5 V with the same capacitance and frequency, the dynamic power becomes:
questions.explanation: Dynamic power is proportional to V_DD²: halving V_DD gives 40 × (1/2)² = 10 mW.

questions.questionText: A processor has 10^6 gates, each with an effective switched capacitance of 10 fF, activity factor α = 0.1, V_DD = 1.2 V and a 1 GHz clock. Its total leakage current is 100 mA. The total power is approximately:
A CMOS gate has V_OH = 4.9 V, V_OL = 0.1 V, V_IH = 3.15 V and V_IL = 1.35 V. Its noise margins are:
A 74LS TTL output (V_OH(min) = 2.7 V, V_OL(max) = 0.5 V) drives a 74HC CMOS input (V_IH(min) = 3.15 V, V_IL(max) = 1.35 V at V_DD = 4.5 V). Which statement is correct?
options: NM_H = −0.45 V, so a valid HIGH is not guaranteed; a pull-up resistor or a 74HCT input is needed
NM_H = 0.45 V, so the interface is reliable
NM_H = 0.7 V, so the interface is reliable
NM_L = −0.85 V, so only the LOW level fails
questions.explanation: NM_H = V_OH − V_IH = 2.7 − 3.15 = −0.45 V (negative, so the HIGH level may be misread), while NM_L = 1.35 − 0.5 = +0.85 V is fine. 74HCT inputs switch at TTL levels (V_IH = 2 V).

questions.questionText: A CMOS gate has t_PHL = 6 ns and t_PLH = 10 ns. Its average propagation delay is:
A ring oscillator is made of 5 identical CMOS inverters connected in a loop, each with propagation delay t_p = 2 ns. Its oscillation frequency is:
questions.explanation: One period needs the edge to travel round the ring twice (once rising, once falling), so T = 2Nt_p = 2 × 5 × 2 ns = 20 ns and f = 1/T = 50 MHz.

questions.questionText: A CMOS gate drives a load C = 50 fF from V_DD = 1.2 V with an average drive current I = 100 µA. Using t_p ≈ C·V_DD/I, its propagation delay is about:
A logic gate dissipates 2 mW and has a propagation delay of 10 ns. Its speed-power (power-delay) product is:
questions.explanation: PDP = P × t_p = 2 × 10⁻³ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ = 20 × 10⁻¹² J = 20 pJ, the energy per switching operation.

questions.questionText: A CMOS output drives a 15 pF load from a 5 V supply with a 1 MHz square wave. The average current drawn from the supply is:
questions.explanation: Each cycle the supply delivers charge Q = C·V_DD = 15 pF × 5 V = 75 pC, so I = Q·f = 75 × 10⁻¹² × 10⁶ = 75 µA.

questions.questionText: A CMOS output has an effective output resistance of 200 Ω, and its 10–90 % rise time (t_r ≈ 2.2RC) must not exceed 20 ns. Wiring adds 5 pF and each driven gate input adds 5 pF. The maximum fan-out is:
questions.explanation: C_max = t_r/(2.2R) = 20 ns/(2.2 × 200 Ω) = 45.5 pF. Subtracting 5 pF of wiring leaves 40.5 pF, and 40.5/5 = 8.1, so at most 8 inputs.

questions.questionText: Each gate on a CMOS chip leaks 1 nA at V_DD = 5 V. For 10^6 gates, the static power is:
In a CMOS process the electron mobility is 2.5 times the hole mobility. For equal pull-up and pull-down drive in an inverter whose nMOS has W/L = 2, the pMOS should have W/L of:
questions.explanation: k is proportional to μ(W/L), so equal k needs (W/L)_p = 2.5 × (W/L)_n = 2.5 × 2 = 5.

questions.questionText: A static CMOS 3-input NAND gate uses how many transistors?
questions.explanation: Every input drives one nMOS and one pMOS: three nMOS in series for the pull-down and three pMOS in parallel for the pull-up, 6 in total.

questions.questionText: A symmetric CMOS inverter (matched nMOS and pMOS) runs from V_DD = 3.3 V. Its switching threshold V_M is:
questions.explanation: With matched devices the pull-up and pull-down are equally strong, so V_M = V_DD/2 = 1.65 V.

questions.questionText: A CMOS inverter has V_DD = 2.5 V, V_tn = 0.5 V, |V_tp| = 0.5 V and k_n = 4k_p. Its switching threshold V_M is:
questions.explanation: r = √(k_p/k_n) = 0.5, so V_M = [V_tn + r(V_DD − |V_tp|)]/(1 + r) = (0.5 + 0.5 × 2)/1.5 = 1.0 V. The stronger nMOS pulls V_M below V_DD/2.

questions.questionText: A CMOS output charges a 10 pF load from 0 V to 5 V. The energy dissipated in the pMOS during this single LOW-to-HIGH transition is:
questions.explanation: The supply delivers C·V² = 10 pF × 25 = 250 pJ; half (½CV² = 125 pJ) is stored on the capacitor and the other 125 pJ is dissipated in the pMOS.

questions.questionText: A chip's power budget allows 1 W of dynamic power. Its capacitance switched (charged and discharged) every clock cycle is 200 pF and V_DD = 1.8 V. The highest clock frequency it can run at is approximately:
A processor dissipates 20 W of dynamic power at 1.2 V and 2 GHz. If it is run at 0.9 V and 1.5 GHz, the dynamic power becomes approximately:
At the switching threshold V_M of a CMOS inverter (input = output = V_M):
options: Both transistors are cut off and the output floats
Both transistors are in saturation and the voltage gain is at its maximum
The nMOS is ohmic and the pMOS is cut off
Both transistors are ohmic and the gain is unity
questions.explanation: At V_M both devices conduct the same saturation current, so the output is very sensitive to the input: the VTC is steepest there.

questions.questionText: As the input of a CMOS inverter rises just above V_tn while the output is still close to V_DD, the operating regions are:
options: nMOS in the ohmic region, pMOS in saturation
nMOS in saturation, pMOS in the ohmic region
nMOS cut off, pMOS in saturation
questions.explanation: The nMOS has a small overdrive but a large V_DS ≈ V_DD, so it is saturated; the pMOS is fully on with only a small |V_DS|, so it is ohmic.

questions.questionText: The unloaded output of a CMOS inverter swings between:
questions.explanation: In each steady state the conducting transistor carries no current, so it drops no voltage and the output reaches the supply rail or ground.

questions.questionText: In a static CMOS 2-input NAND gate:
options: The nMOS transistors are in parallel and the pMOS transistors are in series
The nMOS transistors are in series and the pMOS transistors are in parallel
All four transistors are in series
All four transistors are in parallel
questions.explanation: The output goes LOW only when both series nMOS are on (A = B = 1); either parallel pMOS pulls the output HIGH when any input is 0.

questions.questionText: In a static CMOS 2-input NOR gate, the two pMOS transistors are connected:
options: In series between V_DD and the output
In parallel between V_DD and the output
In series between the output and ground
In parallel between the output and ground
questions.explanation: The output is HIGH only when both inputs are 0, which needs both pMOS on in series; the nMOS are in parallel to ground.

questions.questionText: NAND gates are usually preferred over NOR gates in CMOS design because:
options: A NAND gate needs fewer transistors than a NOR gate
NOR gates cannot be built in CMOS
NAND gates have no dynamic power dissipation
A NOR gate puts the slower pMOS transistors in series, so it needs much wider devices for the same speed
questions.explanation: Both use 2n transistors, but series pMOS (low hole mobility) make the NOR pull-up slow or large, whereas NAND puts the faster nMOS in series.

questions.questionText: In a static CMOS gate the pull-down network has nMOS A and B in series, and this pair is in parallel with nMOS C. The gate output is:
questions.explanation: The pull-down conducts, pulling Y LOW, when A·B + C = 1, so Y is the complement: an AND-OR-INVERT gate.

questions.questionText: The pull-up (pMOS) network of a static CMOS gate is obtained from its pull-down (nMOS) network by:
options: Replacing series connections with parallel ones and parallel connections with series ones
Copying the network exactly using pMOS devices
Reversing the source and drain of each transistor
Adding an inverter at the output
questions.explanation: The pull-up must conduct exactly when the pull-down does not; by De Morgan's theorem this is the dual network with series and parallel exchanged.

questions.questionText: A CMOS transmission gate consists of:
options: An nMOS and a pMOS in series with the same gate signal
A CMOS inverter followed by a buffer
An nMOS and a pMOS in parallel with complementary gate signals, passing both logic levels without threshold loss
questions.explanation: The nMOS passes a strong 0 and the pMOS a strong 1; in parallel they form a bidirectional switch that passes the full 0 to V_DD range.

questions.questionText: A single nMOS pass transistor with its gate at V_DD = 5 V and V_tn = 1 V (body effect neglected) passes a logic 1. Its output node charges to at most:
questions.explanation: The nMOS stops conducting when its V_GS falls to V_tn, so the output rises only to V_DD − V_tn = 5 − 1 = 4 V: an nMOS passes a weak 1.

questions.questionText: The static power dissipation of a CMOS inverter is almost zero because:
options: In either steady state one transistor is off, so no DC path exists from V_DD to ground
The supply current flows only through the gate oxide
The output always sits at V_DD/2
questions.explanation: With the input at 0 or V_DD, one of the series pair is cut off, so only tiny leakage currents flow.

questions.questionText: Short-circuit (crowbar) current in a CMOS inverter:
options: Flows while the input is between V_tn and V_DD − |V_tp|, and grows when input edges are slow
Flows continuously whenever the output is HIGH
Is the main component of static power
Flows only when the load capacitance is zero
questions.explanation: Only while the input passes through the middle range are both transistors on together; slow edges keep them both on longer, so the crowbar current increases.

questions.questionText: Which change does NOT reduce the dynamic power of a CMOS circuit?
options: Stopping the clock to idle blocks (clock gating)
Raising the clock frequency while keeping V_DD constant
questions.explanation: P = α·C·V_DD²·f, so reducing V_DD, C or the activity α lowers power, while a higher f raises it.

questions.questionText: The propagation delay t_PHL of a logic gate is measured:
options: From the 50 % point of the input edge to the 50 % point of the falling output edge
From 10 % to 90 % of the output edge
From 0 V to V_DD of the input edge
From the 50 % point of the input to the 90 % point of the rising output
questions.explanation: Propagation delays are measured between the 50 % points of input and output; 10–90 % intervals define rise and fall times instead.

questions.questionText: The fan-out of a CMOS gate driving other CMOS inputs is limited mainly by:
options: The DC input current drawn by the driven gates
Breakdown of the gate oxide of the driving transistor
The total input capacitance of the driven gates, which slows the output edges
The value of the supply voltage
questions.explanation: CMOS inputs draw practically no DC current, but each adds a few picofarads; too many inputs make the edges too slow.

questions.questionText: Latch-up in a CMOS integrated circuit is caused by:
options: Breakdown of the thin gate oxide by static charge
Running the clock at too low a frequency
A parasitic pnpn (thyristor) structure formed by the wells, substrate and diffusions switching on
questions.explanation: Parasitic npn and pnp transistors in the substrate form an SCR; if triggered, for example by an input driven beyond the rails, it latches a low-resistance path from V_DD to ground.

questions.questionText: An unused input of a CMOS 3-input NAND gate should be:
options: Tied to V_DD, directly or through a resistor
Connected to the gate's own output
questions.explanation: A HIGH on a NAND input does not affect the other inputs; grounding it would force the output permanently HIGH, and a floating input can drift and cause excess current or oscillation.

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing CMOS (74HC) and TTL (74LS) logic is correct?
options: TTL has larger noise margins than CMOS
CMOS inputs draw more current than TTL inputs
TTL works over a wider supply-voltage range than CMOS
CMOS power rises with switching frequency, whereas TTL power stays roughly constant
questions.explanation: CMOS dissipates mainly C·V²·f, so its power grows with frequency, while a TTL gate draws a roughly steady supply current. CMOS also has higher noise margins, near-zero input current and a wider supply range.

questions.questionText: The original 4000-series CMOS logic family can operate from a supply of about:
questions.explanation: The 4000 series accepts roughly 3 to 15 V, unlike 74LS TTL, which requires 5 V ± 5 %.

questions.questionText: A standard six-transistor SRAM cell stores one bit using:
options: Two cross-coupled CMOS inverters plus two access transistors
A pair of bipolar transistors and two resistors
questions.explanation: The two cross-coupled inverters form a latch (4 transistors) and two nMOS access transistors connect it to the bit lines. A MOSFET plus a capacitor is a DRAM cell.

questions.questionText: In a CMOS inverter, the bodies of the transistors are normally connected as:
options: nMOS body to V_DD and pMOS body to ground
nMOS body (p-substrate) to ground and pMOS body (n-well) to V_DD
questions.explanation: Tying the p-substrate to the lowest potential and the n-well to the highest keeps all source and drain junctions reverse biased.

questions.questionText: In an inverter the nMOS has W/L = 2. For a 4-input NAND gate whose worst-case pull-down (four nMOS in series) should match that inverter, each nMOS needs a W/L of about:
questions.explanation: Four equal series resistances add, so each must have one quarter of the inverter's resistance, i.e. four times its W/L: 4 × 2 = 8.

questions.questionText: A static CMOS complex gate implementing Y = NOT(A·B + C) needs how many transistors?
questions.explanation: Each of the three inputs drives one nMOS (pull-down: A and B in series, parallel with C) and one pMOS (the dual pull-up), giving 6 transistors.

questions.questionText: The leakage (static) power of a CMOS chip increases when:
options: The temperature rises or the threshold voltage is reduced
questions.explanation: Sub-threshold leakage grows exponentially as V_T falls and as temperature rises; frequency and capacitance affect dynamic power, not leakage.

questions.questionText: CMOS logic has high noise immunity mainly because:
options: Its inputs draw large currents that swamp noise
It is built from bipolar transistors
Its output levels are close to the rails and its transfer characteristic switches sharply near V_DD/2
Its outputs have very high impedance
questions.explanation: Rail-to-rail outputs and a steep VTC place V_IL and V_IH far from V_OL and V_OH, giving noise margins of roughly 30 % of V_DD.

questions.questionText: For a logic family, the low-level noise margin NM_L is defined as:
questions.explanation: NM_L is how far the worst-case LOW output can rise before it reaches the highest input voltage still read as LOW: V_IL − V_OL. V_OH − V_IH is NM_H.

questions.questionText: In a 2-input CMOS NOR gate each pMOS has an on-resistance of 2 kΩ and the load is 50 fF. Using t_p ≈ 0.69RC, the worst-case LOW-to-HIGH propagation delay is approximately:
questions.explanation: The two pMOS are in series, so R = 4 kΩ and t_pLH = 0.69 × 4 × 10³ × 50 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 1.38 × 10⁻¹⁰ s = 138 ps.

subtopics.title: BJT Small- and Large-Signal Models
subtopics.subtitle: DC models fix the Q-point; r_e, hybrid-π and h-parameter models give the AC gain

concepts.text: Why Two Kinds of Model

A BJT is a non-linear device: its collector current depends exponentially on the base-emitter voltage. Solving an amplifier exactly with that law is impractical, so the analysis is split in two. The DC (large-signal) analysis uses a simple non-linear model to locate the quiescent operating point (Q-point: I_CQ, V_CEQ). The AC (small-signal) analysis then replaces the transistor by a linear circuit whose element values depend on the Q-point, and uses it to find gain, input resistance and output resistance. The total voltage or current at any node is the DC value plus the small AC value superimposed on it.
Large-Signal (DC) Models

The complete large-signal description is the Ebers-Moll model: two ideal diodes (base-emitter and base-collector) placed back to back, each shunted by a dependent current source that carries a fraction (alpha) of the other diode's current. It is valid in all four regions (active, saturation, cut-off and reverse-active) and is what circuit simulators use. In the forward-active region it reduces to I_C = I_S exp(V_BE / V_T), with I_S of the order of 10^-14 A and V_T = 26 mV at room temperature.
For hand calculation the exponential is replaced by piecewise-linear models, one per region:
items: Forward-active: the base-emitter junction is a 0.7 V battery (silicon), the collector is a current source I_C = beta I_B, and I_E = I_C + I_B = (beta + 1) I_B. This is the amplifier model.

Saturation: both junctions forward biased; V_BE is about 0.7 to 0.8 V and V_CE(sat) is about 0.2 V. The collector current is set by the external circuit and is less than beta I_B, so the transistor behaves as a closed switch.
Cut-off: both junctions reverse biased (V_BE below about 0.5 V); all currents are essentially zero and the transistor is an open switch.
Test for saturation: assume active operation, compute I_C = beta I_B, and check V_CE. If V_CE comes out below about 0.2 V (or negative), the assumption is wrong and the transistor is saturated.

concepts.latex: I_C = I_S e^{V_{BE}/V_T}, \qquad I_C = \beta I_B, \qquad I_E = I_C + I_B
concepts.plainText: I_C = I_S·e^(V_BE/V_T);  I_C = β·I_B;  I_E = I_C + I_B

concepts.text: The DC load line joins the two limits of the collector circuit V_CE = V_CC - I_C R_C: the cut-off point (I_C = 0, V_CE = V_CC) and the saturation point (V_CE = 0, I_C = V_CC / R_C). The bias network chooses where on this line the transistor rests; that intersection is the Q-point. For the largest undistorted swing the Q-point is placed near the middle of the load line (V_CEQ about V_CC / 2). The input signal then moves the operating point up and down the line about Q, and the small-signal models describe that movement.
Small-Signal (AC) Models

A signal is small when the AC part of v_BE is only a few millivolts, much less than V_T. The exponential curve is then indistinguishable from its tangent at the Q-point, so the transistor can be replaced by linear resistors and a controlled source. Three equivalent forms are in common use: the r_e model, the hybrid-pi model and the h-parameter model. They give the same answers; they differ only in which quantity is chosen as the control variable and in how the parameters are obtained.
The r_e model (Boylestad) uses the dynamic emitter resistance as its single key parameter:
items: r_e = V_T / I_E = 26 mV / I_E (in mA, giving ohms). At I_E = 1 mA, r_e = 26 ohm.
Looking into the base, the input resistance is beta r_e (more exactly (beta + 1) r_e), because base current is 1/beta of the emitter current.
Common-emitter voltage gain with a bypassed emitter: A_v = -R_C / r_e. With an unbypassed emitter resistor R_E it drops to about -R_C / (r_e + R_E).
Common-base gain is +R_C / r_e; the emitter follower has gain slightly less than 1 and output resistance about r_e.

concepts.text: The hybrid-pi model (Sedra-Smith) uses the base-emitter voltage as the control variable and a transconductance g_m:
items: g_m = I_C / V_T: the slope of the I_C versus V_BE curve at the Q-point; 1 mA gives 38.5 mA/V.
r_pi = beta / g_m = V_T / I_B: the resistance seen between base and emitter; it equals (beta + 1) r_e, approximately beta r_e.
r_o = V_A / I_C: the output resistance from collector to emitter caused by the Early effect (V_A about 50 to 150 V); often ignored when R_C is much smaller than r_o.

The controlled source is g_m v_pi (equivalently beta i_b), so the CE gain is A_v = -g_m (R_C parallel r_o). For high-frequency work the junction capacitances C_pi and C_mu are added to the same model.

concepts.text: The h-parameter model treats the transistor as a two-port network described by measured hybrid parameters. For the common-emitter connection the equations are v_be = h_ie i_b + h_re v_ce and i_c = h_fe i_b + h_oe v_ce. Each parameter is measured with either the output shorted or the input open, which is why data sheets can quote them directly. In simplified analysis h_re and h_oe are usually neglected, leaving only h_ie (input resistance) and h_fe (current gain), which then correspond exactly to r_pi and beta of the hybrid-pi model.

concepts.text: Worked Example

A silicon BJT with beta = 100 is biased at I_C = 1 mA and drives a collector resistor R_C = 5 kΩ with the emitter bypassed. Transconductance g_m = I_C / V_T = 1 mA / 26 mV = 38.5 mA/V. Input resistance r_pi = beta / g_m = 100 / 0.0385 = 2.6 kΩ. In r_e terms, I_E is about 1.01 mA so r_e is about 26 ohm and beta r_e is again about 2.6 kΩ. The voltage gain is A_v = -g_m R_C = -0.0385 x 5000 = -192, and the r_e model gives the same figure: -R_C / r_e = -5000 / 26 = -192. If the data sheet instead quoted h_ie = 2.6 kΩ and h_fe = 100, the h-parameter gain -h_fe R_C / h_ie would also be -192.
Going Deeper: Deriving and Applying the BJT Models

The transconductance comes straight from the exponential law. Differentiating I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) with respect to V_BE gives I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) / V_T, which is simply I_C / V_T. The same law shows that V_BE rises by V_T ln 10, about 60 mV, for every tenfold increase in collector current, and by V_T ln 2, about 18 mV, when the current doubles. Expanding e^(v_be/V_T) as 1 + v_be/V_T + ... shows why the linear model needs v_be much smaller than V_T: at 5 mV the neglected square term is already about 10 % of the linear term.

concepts.plainText: g_m = di_C/dv_BE = I_C / V_T;  ΔV_BE = V_T·ln(I_C2 / I_C1)

concepts.text: In the Ebers-Moll equations each junction current follows the diode law, I_F = I_ES (e^(V_BE/V_T) − 1) for the emitter diode and I_R = I_CS (e^(V_BC/V_T) − 1) for the collector diode. The terminal currents are I_C = α_F I_F − I_R and I_E = I_F − α_R I_R. Reciprocity requires α_F I_ES = α_R I_CS = I_S. Because the collector is large and lightly doped, α_R is small (roughly 0.1 to 0.5), so the reverse-active current gain β_R = α_R / (1 − α_R) is usually below 1; this is why a transistor with collector and emitter swapped is a poor amplifier.

rows: V_BE ≈ 0.8 V, V_CE(sat) ≈ 0.2 V, I_C < β I_B
Roles swapped; β_R well below β_F

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - is the transistor saturated?
Given: V_BB = 3.3 V, R_B = 10 kΩ, V_CC = 5 V, R_C = 1 kΩ, β = 80
Assume active: I_B = (3.3 − 0.7) / 10 kΩ = 0.26 mA
  I_C = β I_B = 80 × 0.26 mA = 20.8 mA
  V_CE = 5 − 20.8 mA × 1 kΩ = −15.8 V  -> impossible
So the BJT is saturated: V_CE = 0.2 V
  I_C(sat) = (5 − 0.2) / 1 kΩ = 4.8 mA
  Forced beta = I_C / I_B = 4.8 / 0.26 = 18.5 (less than 80)
  Minimum base current for saturation = 4.8 mA / 80 = 60 µA
Converting between the model families (common-emitter h-parameters on the left):
items: h_fe = β and h_ie = r_π, so g_m = h_fe / h_ie; for example h_fe = 100 and h_ie = 2.5 kΩ give g_m = 40 mA/V, which at V_T = 25 mV means I_C = 1 mA.
h_oe = 1 / r_o, so a data-sheet h_oe of 20 µS corresponds to r_o = 50 kΩ in the hybrid-π model.
Common-base values follow from the CE ones: h_ib = h_ie / (1 + h_fe), which is r_e, and h_fb = −h_fe / (1 + h_fe), which is −α.
h_re and h_fe are dimensionless, h_ie is in ohms and h_oe is in siemens; that mix of units is why they are called hybrid parameters.

concepts.latex: A_i = \frac{h_{fe}}{1 + h_{oe} R_L}, \quad Z_i = h_{ie} - h_{re} A_i R_L
concepts.plainText: A_i = h_fe / (1 + h_oe·R_L);  Z_i = h_ie − h_re·A_i·R_L = h_ie − h_re·h_fe·R_L / (1 + h_oe·R_L)

concepts.text: Writing the CE gain as A_v = −g_m R_C = −I_C R_C / V_T shows that the gain equals the DC voltage dropped across R_C divided by V_T: a 5 V drop gives about −200 at V_T = 25 mV, whatever the individual values of I_C and R_C. The largest gain a single transistor can give, with only its own r_o as load, is the intrinsic gain g_m r_o = V_A / V_T, a few thousand. At high frequencies the hybrid-π model adds C_π between base and emitter and C_µ between base and collector, and the transition frequency where the short-circuit current gain falls to 1 is f_T = g_m / (2π (C_π + C_µ)).

Frequent slips in model questions: using r_e = 26 mV / I_E with I_E in amperes and quoting the answer in ohms without the factor 1000; taking g_m = I_B / V_T instead of I_C / V_T; forgetting R_L in parallel with R_C in the AC load; using −R_C / r_e when R_E is not bypassed; and trusting I_C = β I_B without first checking that V_CE is above V_CE(sat).

formulas.latex: I_C = \beta I_B, \qquad V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_C R_C
formulas.plainText: I_C = β·I_B;  V_CE = V_CC − I_C·R_C (DC load line)
g_m = I_C / V_T;  r_π = β / g_m;  r_o = V_A / I_C

formulas.latex: v_{be} = h_{ie} i_b + h_{re} v_{ce}, \qquad i_c = h_{fe} i_b + h_{oe} v_{ce}
formulas.plainText: v_be = h_ie·i_b + h_re·v_ce;  i_c = h_fe·i_b + h_oe·v_ce

notes.text: Two numbers unlock most model MCQs: V_T = 26 mV at room temperature and V_BE = 0.7 V. From them, r_e = 26 mV / I_E, g_m = I_C / 26 mV, and r_π = β / g_m. Check the units: I_E in mA gives r_e in ohms; I_C in mA gives g_m in mA/V.

Do not mix the two analyses. In the AC model every DC source is a short circuit (V_CC to ground) and coupling or bypass capacitors are shorts; in the DC model every capacitor is an open circuit. Using R_C in a DC calculation but forgetting that the AC collector load is R_C in parallel with R_L is a common slip.

The letters in h-parameters spell their meaning: i = input, r = reverse, f = forward, o = output, and the second subscript (e, b or c) names the common terminal. h_fe is simply the AC beta and h_ie the AC input resistance; h_re and h_oe are small enough to drop in most exam problems.

formulas.title: Dynamic emitter resistance
formulas.description: I_E is the DC emitter current at the Q-point; with I_E in mA the result is in ohms, and the base sees β r_e.

formulas.title: Transconductance
formulas.description: V_T = kT/q ≈ 26 mV at 300 K; g_m is the slope of the I_C–V_BE curve at the Q-point and equals 1 / r_e.

formulas.title: Hybrid-π input resistance
formulas.description: Resistance seen between base and emitter in the small-signal model; it is the same quantity as h_ie and approximately β r_e.

formulas.title: CE small-signal voltage gain
formulas.description: Gain of a common-emitter stage with the emitter bypassed; R_C should be replaced by R_C ∥ R_L when a load is connected, and the minus sign marks the 180° phase inversion.

formulas.title: DC load line
formulas.description: Straight line between cut-off (I_C = 0, V_CE = V_CC) and saturation (V_CE = 0, I_C = V_CC / R_C); the Q-point lies where the bias circuit puts it on this line.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of the large-signal model and of the small-signal model of a BJT?
flashcards.back: The large-signal (DC) model finds the Q-point using V_BE = 0.7 V and I_C = β I_B. The small-signal (AC) model linearises the transistor around that Q-point to compute gain and impedances.

flashcards.front: Give g_m, r_π and r_e for a BJT at I_C = 1 mA with β = 100.
flashcards.back: g_m = 1 mA / 26 mV = 38.5 mA/V; r_π = β / g_m ≈ 2.6 kΩ; r_e = 26 mV / I_E ≈ 26 Ω.

flashcards.front: Name the four CE h-parameters and what each represents.
flashcards.back: h_ie: input impedance (≈ r_π); h_re: reverse voltage feedback ratio (≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁴); h_fe: forward current gain (= β); h_oe: output admittance (= 1 / r_o).

flashcards.front: Which DC voltages describe the saturation model of a silicon BJT?
flashcards.back: V_BE ≈ 0.7 to 0.8 V and V_CE(sat) ≈ 0.2 V, with I_C fixed by the external circuit and smaller than β I_B.

questions.questionText: A BJT is biased at I_C = 2 mA at room temperature (V_T = 26 mV). Its small-signal transconductance g_m is approximately:
questions.explanation: g_m = I_C / V_T = 2 mA / 26 mV ≈ 77 mA/V. Doubling the bias current doubles g_m, which is why 1 mA gives the familiar 38.5 mA/V.

questions.questionText: In the common-emitter h-parameter model, the parameter h_fe represents the transistor's:
options: Input impedance with the output shorted
Forward current gain with the output shorted
Output admittance with the input open
questions.explanation: h_fe = i_c / i_b measured with v_ce = 0 (output shorted) is the AC forward current gain, identical to β. h_ie is the input impedance, h_re the reverse ratio and h_oe the output admittance.

questions.questionText: To determine the quiescent operating point (I_CQ, V_CEQ) of a BJT amplifier, the appropriate model is the:
options: Hybrid-π model with g_m and r_π
r_e model with r_e = 26 mV / I_E
Piecewise-linear DC model with V_BE = 0.7 V and I_C = β I_B
questions.explanation: The Q-point is a DC (large-signal) quantity, so the DC model with a 0.7 V base-emitter drop and I_C = β I_B is used. The hybrid-π, r_e and h-parameter models are small-signal models whose values depend on the Q-point found first.

questions.questionText: A common-emitter amplifier with a fully bypassed emitter resistor operates at I_E = 2 mA and has R_C = 2.6 kΩ (no external load). Using the r_e model, its voltage gain is about:
questions.explanation: r_e = 26 mV / 2 mA = 13 Ω, so A_v = −R_C / r_e = −2600 / 13 = −200. The negative sign indicates the 180° phase inversion of a CE stage.

questions.questionText: The Ebers-Moll model of a BJT is valid in which operating regions?
options: All four: forward-active, saturation, cut-off and reverse-active
questions.explanation: The Ebers-Moll model uses the full diode law for both junctions with two dependent sources, so it describes all four regions; piecewise models are region-specific.

questions.questionText: The Ebers-Moll large-signal model of a BJT consists of:
options: A single diode in series with a resistor
Two back-to-back diodes, each paralleled by a current-controlled current source
A voltage-controlled voltage source and an output resistance
A 0.7 V battery and a resistor r_e only
questions.explanation: Ebers-Moll represents the base-emitter and base-collector junctions as diodes, each shunted by a dependent source carrying α times the other junction's diode current.

questions.questionText: A silicon BJT in the active region has I_S = 10^-14 A. Using I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) with V_T = 26 mV, the collector current at V_BE = 0.65 V is about:
For a BJT obeying I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) with V_T = 26 mV, by how much must V_BE increase to raise I_C tenfold?
questions.explanation: ΔV_BE = V_T ln(10) = 26 mV × 2.303 = 59.9 mV, about 60 mV per decade of current.

questions.questionText: A BJT is operating at I_C = 1 mA. With V_T = 26 mV, the increase in V_BE required to double the collector current to 2 mA is about:
In a base-driven switch, V_BB = 5 V is applied through R_B = 20 kΩ; the collector is fed from V_CC = 10 V through R_C = 2 kΩ, and β = 100 (V_BE = 0.7 V, V_CE(sat) = 0.2 V). The transistor is:
options: Active, with I_C ≈ 21.5 mA and V_CE ≈ −33 V
Active, with I_C ≈ 2.15 mA and V_CE ≈ 5.7 V
Saturated, with I_C ≈ 4.9 mA and V_CE ≈ 0.2 V
Cut off, with I_C ≈ 0 and V_CE = 10 V
questions.explanation: I_B = (5 − 0.7)/20 kΩ = 215 µA, so β I_B = 21.5 mA would need V_CE = 10 − 43 = −33 V, which is impossible. The BJT saturates: I_C = (10 − 0.2)/2 kΩ = 4.9 mA.

questions.questionText: A fixed-bias silicon BJT has V_CC = 12 V, R_B = 565 kΩ, R_C = 3 kΩ and β = 100 (V_BE = 0.7 V). The Q-point (I_CQ, V_CEQ) is:
A saturated BJT switch carries I_C = 5 mA with a base current of 0.5 mA. Its forced beta is:
questions.explanation: Forced beta = I_C/I_B = 5 mA / 0.5 mA = 10; in saturation this is always below the active-region β.

questions.questionText: In the large-signal piecewise model, a BJT in cut-off is represented between collector and emitter by:
questions.explanation: In cut-off both junctions are reverse biased and all currents are practically zero, so the collector-emitter path is an open switch.

questions.questionText: When a BJT is operated in the reverse-active mode (collector and emitter roles interchanged), its current gain is:
options: Much smaller than the forward β, usually below 1
Infinite, because the base current becomes zero
questions.explanation: The lightly doped, large collector is a poor emitter, so α_R is small (about 0.1 to 0.5) and β_R = α_R/(1 − α_R) is usually less than 1.

questions.questionText: In the Ebers-Moll model, reciprocity requires α_F I_ES = α_R I_CS = I_S. A transistor has I_S = 2 × 10^-15 A and reverse alpha α_R = 0.4. Its collector-diode saturation current I_CS is:
questions.explanation: I_CS = I_S/α_R = 2 × 10^-15 / 0.4 = 5 × 10^-15 A; the collector diode has the larger saturation current because α_R is small.

questions.questionText: A CE stage (emitter bypassed) runs at I_C = 2 mA with V_T = 25 mV and Early voltage V_A = 100 V. R_C = 5 kΩ and the load R_L = 5 kΩ. Including r_o, the voltage gain is about:
At room temperature (V_T = 25 mV), a BJT biased at I_C = 0.5 mA has a transconductance of:
questions.explanation: g_m = I_C/V_T = 0.5 mA / 25 mV = 20 mA/V.

questions.questionText: A BJT with β = 150 is biased at I_C = 1.5 mA (V_T = 25 mV). Its hybrid-π input resistance r_π is:
The quiescent base current of a BJT is 10 µA. With V_T = 26 mV, the small-signal resistance r_π is:
questions.explanation: r_π = V_T/I_B = 26 mV / 10 µA = 2.6 kΩ.

questions.questionText: A BJT has an Early voltage V_A = 100 V and is biased at I_C = 2 mA. Its small-signal output resistance r_o is:
questions.explanation: r_o = V_A/I_C = 100 V / 2 mA = 50 kΩ.

questions.questionText: For a BJT with V_A = 50 V at room temperature (V_T = 25 mV), the intrinsic voltage gain g_m r_o is:
questions.explanation: g_m r_o = (I_C/V_T)(V_A/I_C) = V_A/V_T = 50/0.025 = 2000, independent of the bias current.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the hybrid-π parameters of a BJT is correct?
options: g_m depends only on I_C and temperature, not on β
r_π is independent of the bias current
r_o decreases when the Early voltage increases
questions.explanation: g_m = I_C/V_T contains no β; r_π = β/g_m falls as I_C rises, and r_o = V_A/I_C grows with V_A.

questions.questionText: A BJT with β = 99 is biased at I_E = 2.5 mA (V_T = 25 mV). Its r_e and r_π are respectively:
The small-signal (linear) models of a BJT are valid only when:
options: The AC base-emitter voltage is larger than 0.7 V
The AC base-emitter voltage is much smaller than V_T (a few millivolts)
questions.explanation: The exponential i_C-v_BE law is well approximated by its tangent only if v_be ≪ V_T ≈ 25 mV.

questions.questionText: The thermal voltage V_T = kT/q at T = 300 K (k = 1.38 × 10^-23 J/K, q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C) is about:
In the high-frequency hybrid-π model of a BJT, the capacitances C_π and C_µ represent:
options: The base-emitter and base-collector junction capacitances
The coupling and bypass capacitors of the amplifier
The collector-emitter and collector-substrate capacitances only
The capacitances of the DC power supply
questions.explanation: C_π (diffusion plus depletion) sits between base and emitter, C_µ (depletion) between base and collector; external coupling and bypass capacitors are separate.

questions.questionText: A BJT biased at I_C = 1 mA (V_T = 25 mV) has C_π = 11 pF and C_µ = 1 pF. Its transition frequency f_T = g_m / (2π(C_π + C_µ)) is about:
questions.explanation: g_m = 1 mA/25 mV = 40 mA/V; f_T = 0.04 / (2π × 12 pF) = 531 MHz (using C_π alone would give 579 MHz).

questions.questionText: When drawing the small-signal AC equivalent circuit of a BJT amplifier, the DC supply V_CC and the large coupling/bypass capacitors are replaced by:
questions.explanation: An ideal DC source has zero AC voltage and a large capacitor has negligible reactance at signal frequency, so both become shorts in the AC model.

questions.questionText: A BJT is biased at I_C = 2 mA (V_T = 25 mV) and a 5 mV peak signal is applied between base and emitter. The resulting peak AC collector current is about:
questions.explanation: i_c = g_m v_be = (2 mA/25 mV) × 5 mV = 80 mA/V × 5 mV = 0.4 mA.

questions.questionText: The CE h-parameter h_oe is measured in:
questions.explanation: h_oe = i_c/v_ce with the input open; a current divided by a voltage is an admittance, in siemens.

questions.questionText: Which pair of CE h-parameters is dimensionless?
questions.explanation: h_re is a voltage ratio and h_fe a current ratio, so both are pure numbers; h_ie is in ohms and h_oe in siemens.

questions.questionText: A CE amplifier uses a transistor with h_fe = 120 and h_ie = 2 kΩ. R_C = 4 kΩ and R_L = 4 kΩ (h_re and h_oe neglected). The voltage gain is:
questions.explanation: AC load = R_C ∥ R_L = 2 kΩ; A_v = −h_fe R_ac/h_ie = −120 × 2 kΩ/2 kΩ = −120.

questions.questionText: A CE transistor has h_fe = 100 and h_oe = 25 µS and drives a load R_L = 4 kΩ. Its current gain A_i = h_fe/(1 + h_oe R_L) is about:
A CE transistor has h_ie = 1.1 kΩ, h_re = 2.5 × 10^-4, h_fe = 50 and h_oe = 25 µS, with R_L = 1 kΩ. Its exact input impedance Z_i = h_ie − h_re h_fe R_L/(1 + h_oe R_L) is about:
questions.explanation: h_oe R_L = 0.025; h_re h_fe R_L/(1.025) = 2.5 × 10^-4 × 50 × 1000/1.025 = 12.2 Ω; Z_i = 1100 − 12.2 = 1088 Ω ≈ 1.09 kΩ. Adding the term instead of subtracting it gives 1.11 kΩ, which is wrong.

questions.questionText: A transistor data sheet gives h_fe = 100 and h_ie = 2.5 kΩ at the operating point. Taking V_T = 25 mV, the collector bias current is about:
questions.explanation: g_m = h_fe/h_ie = 100/2.5 kΩ = 40 mA/V; I_C = g_m V_T = 40 mA/V × 25 mV = 1 mA.

questions.questionText: A transistor has CE current gain h_fe = 99. Its common-base short-circuit current gain h_fb is:
A transistor has h_ie = 2 kΩ and h_fe = 99 in the CE configuration. Its common-base input resistance h_ib is about:
questions.explanation: h_ib = h_ie/(1 + h_fe) = 2000/100 = 20 Ω; this is the emitter resistance r_e.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the h-parameter model of a BJT is NOT correct?
options: Its values depend on the Q-point
It remains accurate at high frequencies without any added capacitances
h_ie and h_fe correspond to r_π and β of the hybrid-π model
h_re and h_oe are often neglected in approximate analysis
questions.explanation: Data-sheet h-parameters are low-frequency, real-valued quantities; they ignore junction capacitances, so they are not valid at high frequencies. The other statements are true.

questions.questionText: A CE stage runs at I_C = 1 mA (V_T = 25 mV) with R_C = 5 kΩ and no external load. The transistor's h_oe is 20 µS. Including h_oe, the voltage gain is about:

A voltage-divider CE amplifier has V_CC = 12 V, R1 = 40 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ (fully bypassed), R_C = 4 kΩ and R_L = 4 kΩ. Using the approximate analysis (base current neglected, V_BE = 0.7 V, V_T = 25 mV), the voltage gain is about:
A CE amplifier has R_C = 4.7 kΩ and an unbypassed emitter resistor R_E = 470 Ω. At the Q-point r_e = 13 Ω. The voltage gain is about:
A CE stage with R_C = 10 kΩ has an unbypassed emitter resistance R_E = 1 kΩ, which is much larger than r_e. Its voltage gain is approximately:
questions.explanation: When R_E ≫ r_e, A_v ≈ −R_C/R_E = −10 kΩ/1 kΩ = −10, nearly independent of the transistor.

questions.questionText: A BJT with β = 99 has r_e = 25 Ω and an unbypassed emitter resistor R_E = 500 Ω. The resistance looking into its base is about:

A CE amplifier has an unloaded-source voltage gain A_v = −150, bias resistance R_B = 10 kΩ and r_π = 2.5 kΩ. It is driven by a source with internal resistance R_s = 1 kΩ. The overall gain v_o/v_s is about:
questions.explanation: R_in = R_B ∥ r_π = 10k ∥ 2.5k = 2 kΩ; A_vs = A_v × R_in/(R_in + R_s) = −150 × 2/3 = −100 (using r_π alone gives −107).

questions.questionText: A CE amplifier has R_C = 10 kΩ and the transistor's r_o = 40 kΩ. Its output resistance (looking back into the collector node) is:
The phase difference between the input and output voltages of a common-emitter amplifier at mid-band frequencies is:
questions.explanation: A rise in base voltage raises i_c, increasing the drop across R_C, so the collector voltage falls: the CE stage inverts (negative gain, 180°).

questions.questionText: If the emitter bypass capacitor of a CE amplifier opens (becomes disconnected), then:
options: The voltage gain rises and the input resistance falls
The voltage gain falls and the input resistance rises
Both the voltage gain and input resistance rise
The DC Q-point shifts into saturation
questions.explanation: Without the bypass, R_E appears in the AC emitter circuit: gain drops to about −R_C/(r_e + R_E) and base input resistance rises to (β + 1)(r_e + R_E). The DC bias is unchanged because the capacitor is open for DC anyway.

questions.questionText: In a bypassed CE stage the quiescent voltage drop across R_C is 5 V. With V_T = 25 mV, the voltage gain magnitude (no load) is:
questions.explanation: |A_v| = g_m R_C = I_C R_C/V_T = 5 V/25 mV = 200, whatever the separate values of I_C and R_C.

questions.questionText: An emitter follower has R_E = 1 kΩ (no external load) and r_e = 25 Ω. Its voltage gain is about:
questions.explanation: A_v = R_E/(R_E + r_e) = 1000/1025 = 0.976: slightly less than one with no phase inversion.

questions.questionText: A common-base amplifier runs at I_E = 0.5 mA (V_T = 25 mV). Its input resistance looking into the emitter is about:
questions.explanation: R_in(CB) ≈ r_e = V_T/I_E = 25 mV/0.5 mA = 50 Ω, which is why the CB stage has a very low input resistance.
